docs.title: modeling-api
docs.text:
Guided for analysts · exact for data scientists · honest uncertainty · one safe platform

v0.4: Guided mode and integrations

Analysts get Guided mode: templates, questions instead of a column mapper, beliefs as ROI ranges and lift tests, a sanity scorecard, what-if sliders and forecasts. Other applications get endpoints promoted through the scorecard, code snippets, signed webhooks, embeddable charts, Google Sheets and an Atlas budget optimiser. Every number on this page was measured on a laptop running the whole stack (M3 verification); the cloud pieces are tested against fakes, and the study with five non-technical testers is still to come.

docs.title: Trustworthy models,from spreadsheet to endpoint.
docs.text:
modeling-api fits Bayesian and classical models of data with named dimensions (market × channel × week, store × product × day, household × trip) and answers questions with them in the units your business uses. An analyst uploads a spreadsheet and gets a report, a sanity scorecard and instant what-if sliders. A data scientist writes a small spec or a few lines of Python and gets the same model behind a versioned endpoint, with the fitted preprocessing replayed exactly on every call. Every run happens in a fresh sandbox, and every result says how sure it is.

Your first MMM in Guided mode Quickstart for data scientists Why modeling-api?

docs.title: Two ways in, one model
docs.text: Both edit the same ModelSpec: every Guided screen has View as YAML, and an expert's changes come back to Guided mode intact. Who it is for, and who it is not for.

docs.title: Analysts
docs.text:
Upload → report → scenario in minutes, with honest uncertainty.

  • Pick what you want to learn; answer "which column is revenue?" (the platform suggests the answer and says why).
  • Say what you already believe ("TV returns 1.5 to 4 per euro") or enter a lift test.
  • Read a report in plain words, with a sanity scorecard that tells you whether to trust it.
  • Drag what-if sliders: answers in your browser, with a range that stays honest when several channels move at once. "Run exact" asks the full model.
  • Share a live chart or put the model in a Google Sheet.

Your first analysis in Guided mode

docs.title: Data scientists
docs.text:
Any PyMC, scikit-learn or forecasting model. Preprocessing replayed exactly. Endpoints in one click.

  • A PyMC model is one build() method, an sklearn model one estimator(); built-in marketing-mix, forecasting, demand and choice models are ready to use.
  • Steps learn on the training data only and are replayed, never refitted, at score time: forecasts, new markets, counterfactuals.
  • Uncertainty is first-class: draws, quantiles or intervals, with the aggregations that are valid for each.
  • Promote a version to an endpoint through the scorecard gate; copy a snippet for Python, TypeScript, curl, R, Apps Script, Atlas or a notebook.

Quickstart: zero to first model

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Your data<br/>CSV · Parquet · MFF ·<br/>Meridian · BayesInsight"] --> I["Sandboxed ingest<br/>checked, profiled,<br/>dims and roles"]
    Q["Guided answers<br/>or a YAML spec"] --> V{{"Static checks<br/>before any compute"}}
    I --> V
    V --> F["Fit in a fresh sandbox<br/>preprocessing learned<br/>on train only"]
    F --> B[("Signed bundle<br/>states · posterior ·<br/>scorecard · grids")]
    B --> R["Report and<br/>what-if sliders"]
    B --> E["Endpoint<br/>gated on the scorecard"]
    E --> S["Sheets · BI embeds ·<br/>webhooks · Atlas ·<br/>Python, TS, R"]
  1. Your data stays labelled. The upload becomes an xr.Dataset with named dims, roles and units; nothing downstream is positional.
  2. Mistakes fail early. A spec that would leak the holdout, a forecast past what the model supports, a market the model has never seen: typed errors, before any compute.
  3. Fitting learns, scoring replays. Every preprocessing step stores what it learned, so a forecast or a new market goes through exactly the same transformations, then back into your units.
  4. Results are checked twice. Outputs are verified against the storage's own checksums and signed; the scorecard checks convergence, holdout error and plausibility.
  5. Other tools connect to an endpoint, not a file. Promote a better model and every integration uses it; roll back with one call.

docs.title: Your first MMM in Guided mode
docs.text:
The whole journey of a geo marketing-mix model, from a spreadsheet of weekly spend and revenue by region to a budget scenario. The times are what an automated "tester" took on a laptop, almost all of it the platform working: 135 seconds from upload to scenario.

  1. Choose "Geo marketing mix" and drop your CSV on the page. Each column is profiled in your browser; the platform suggests which column is revenue, which are spend, and why. (5 s)
  2. Say what you believe, if anything: an ROI range per channel, a lift test. Preview what this means shows it in business units before any fitting. (22 s, optional)
  3. Fit the model. Plain-language progress; the model is tested on weeks it has not seen, then refitted on everything. (80 s)
  4. Read the results: ROI and share per channel with 90% ranges, and the sanity scorecard, each check with what to do next. (instant)
  5. Ask "what if": move search +20% and see the change in revenue with its range at once; Run exact confirms it with the full model. (30 s with the exact run and a forecast)
  6. Share it: put the model live as an endpoint, or share a chart by link.

The full tutorial, with screenshots · From a spreadsheet to a draft, with curl

Templates: start from the question, not the model.

Your data: suggested answers, each with its reason.

Beliefs: ROI ranges and lift tests, previewed in business units.

docs.title: What's new in v0.4
docs.text:
• Guided mode

    Four templates (geo marketing mix, weekly forecast, demand by store, customer choice), role detection, MFF and Meridian presets, drafts you can open as YAML, and a lock that keeps a project Guided-only.

    Tutorial

  • Business priors and lift tests

    ROI or contribution-share ranges translated into model priors in a sandbox, with a prior-predictive preview; experiments enter the likelihood as calibration.

    Guided modelling

  • Sanity scorecard and promotion gate

    Convergence, holdout error and coverage, plausibility and data checks, each in plain words. Pass goes live, warn needs an admin's audited reason, fail is blocked.

    The gate

  • What-if, forecasts, counterfactuals

    Sliders over response curves precomputed per posterior draw, so bands stay joint and honest; "Run exact" scores the full model with common random numbers.

    What if…

  • Endpoints, aliases and snippets

    A stable alias per use, history and rollback, a frozen input contract with an example call, score:<alias> tokens, and generated code in seven flavours.

    Integrations hub

  • Signed webhooks

    run.*, model.version.ready, endpoint.promoted, score.completed: HMAC-signed, retried, logged and replayable, through an SSRF guard.

    Receive webhooks

  • Embeds and static renders

    Read-only, expiring chart links for Notion, Slack, Looker Studio or Power BI, and PNG, SVG or PDF rendered in the sandbox.

    Embed a chart

  • Atlas and Google Sheets

    RemoteModel makes an endpoint an Atlas model for budget optimisation; an Apps Script writes a forecast into a sheet every morning.

    Optimise a budget · Connect Sheets

  • BayesInsight and Meridian data

    BayesInsight's model_def.json runs as a built-in model or maps onto the geo MMM, with every unsupported feature reported, never dropped.

    Import a BayesInsight model

  • Sign-up and the data lifecycle

    Self-service workspaces with e-mail verification and abuse controls, GDPR export, tenant deletion that purges every store, and a Cloud Armor policy.

    Deleting and exporting data

  • A customer-choice model

    choice.multinomial_logit, a conditional logit with household effects, and categorical holdout metrics: hit rate against always guessing the favourite, log score, Brier.

    Use cases

  • Client and CLI for all of it

    api.endpoint("…").score(ds) returns an xarray.Dataset; mapi endpoints, webhooks, plots, guided, priors and tenant cover the rest from a terminal.

    The Python client

docs.title: Connect it to everything
docs.text:
Integrations: Sheets, BI and webhooks in a few steps. Endpoints: one alias, every promotion and rollback with its reason. Snippets: Python, TypeScript, curl, R, Apps Script, Atlas, notebook. Embeds: a read-only chart for a dashboard or a doc, revocable at any time.

schema = geo_mmm.schema()
print(sorted(schema.snapshot.input_schema.vars))

    {"spend_local": (("market", "channel", "date"), np.array([[[1200.0], [5300.0]]]))},
    coords={"market": ["de"], "channel": ["search", "tv"], "date": ["2025-12-30"]},
)

docs.title: The core idea: fit with preprocessing, score with the same preprocessing
docs.text:
The same pipeline object runs at fit time and at score time. At fit time each step learns its state from the training data; at score time it replays that state. Steps that look back in time store a small per-group tail, so a forecast sees exactly the history the model was fitted on.

flowchart LR
    subgraph FIT["Fit (once)"]
        direction LR
        A["Daily spend & revenue<br/>local currency"] --> B["fx_convert<br/>(side table)"]
        B --> C["resample<br/>daily → weekly"]
        C --> S{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
        S --> D["mean_scale<br/><i>learns scale(geo, channel)</i>"]
        D --> E["lag_tensor<br/><i>stores last 6 weeks per geo</i>"]
        E --> M["model.fit"]
    end
    M --> BUN[("Bundle<br/>states · context tails · posterior<br/>hashes · no pickle")]
    subgraph SCORE["Score (any time)"]
        direction LR
        F["Next quarter's plan<br/>or a new market"] --> G["same steps,<br/><b>replayed</b> state"]
        G --> H["model.score"]
        H --> I["inverse → weekly EUR<br/>summaries · your names"]
    end
    BUN --> G
What you writeWhat the platform doesWhat you get back 
pipeline:
  - {id: to_eur, use: core.fx_convert@^1, with: {vars: [y, spend], table: fx, ...}}
  - {id: weekly, use: core.resample@^1,   with: {dim: time, freq: W-SUN, how: sum}}
  - {id: scale,  use: core.mean_scale@^1, with: {vars: [spend], over: [time]}}
  - {id: lags,   use: core.lag_tensor@^1, with: {vars: [spend], along: time, within: [geo], l_max: 6}}
model:
  use: mmm.hierarchical_geo@^1.3
  fit: {mode: evaluate_then_refit}
  1. Checks the whole spec statically: names, dims, settings, units at every stage, where the split happens and whether any step would learn from the holdout (LEAKAGE_RISK).
  2. Fits each stateful step on the training weeks only, fits the model, then scores the holdout through the same path a forecast uses and records the metrics.
  3. Refits on all weeks so forecasts start from the latest data, and writes a bundle with every state, context tail and hash.
  • Forecasts in weekly EUR, not "model units": scaling is inverted, and inversion stops at the weekly resample because daily values cannot be recovered from weekly sums. The output says so in its output_space attribute.
  • A new market drawn from the fitted hyperprior, honestly wider than a known one.
  • What-if deltas that share their noise with the baseline (common random numbers), so the delta reflects the change, not sampling noise.

The same model in plain Python, without any server; every snippet on this site is executed by the test suite:

from mapi_sdk import fit_spec

bundle = fit_spec(spec, data, registry=registry, raw_schema=schema)
print(bundle.metrics.values)  # holdout metrics, in units sold: {'rmse': ..., 'mape': ..., ...}
print(bundle.metrics.n_holdout)  # 48 cells: 3 stores x 2 skus x 8 weeks

from mapi_spec import ErrorCode, MapiError


def try_score(request_yaml: str, payload: xr.Dataset) -> ErrorCode:
    try:
        score_bundle(bundle, request_yaml, payload, registry=registry)
    except MapiError as err:
        print(err.code, "-", err)
        return err.code
    raise AssertionError("expected a typed error")


FORECAST = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
"""

# 1. a forecast without next month's promotions: promo is future_required
code_1 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.drop_vars("promo"))

# 2. quantiles are per cell, so "total over all stores" would be a made-up number
code_2 = try_score(FORECAST + "output: {aggregate: {over: [store]}}\n", plan)

# 3. a product outside the fitted range: sku is a fixed dim
code_3 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.assign_coords(sku=["apples", "kiwis"]))

docs.title: Secure by design
docs.text:
The platform is built to run models and data from people it does not trust. The controls that matter most are not settings you can forget to turn on: they are how it works. The security model says what each one stops, and what is still to be verified in the cloud.

  • A fresh sandbox per run

    Every ingest, fit, score and render runs in its own sandbox (a microVM on Cloud Run Jobs), with no secrets and no network but signed URLs to its own objects. Placement by trust tier is enforced in code.

  • Tenants never see each other

    PostgreSQL row-level security on every table, pinned per transaction and failing closed; roles checked at every request; operators manage the platform without reading tenant data.

  • Outputs are claims

    A run's outputs are checked against the store's own hashes and generations, copied where runs cannot write, and signed. Download links are minted only after the signature verifies.

  • Integrations that cannot be turned against you

    Webhooks are HMAC-signed and sent through an SSRF guard that pins the checked address; embed links show platform recipes only, carry no credential and can be revoked; snippets never contain a secret.

  • Compute you can see and cap

    Quotas in vCPU-seconds per token, tenant and platform, per-token budgets for endpoint callers, a cost on every run, a global spend cap and an audited kill switch.

  • No pickle, anywhere

    Bundles are single zarr zips plus JSON sidecars; native models are skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON. Every file carries CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256, and reading verifies them.

docs.title: Run it for many teams
docs.text:
One deployment serves many organisations. People sign up or sign in with their own identity provider, work in the projects they have a role in, and see what their compute costs; operators look after the platform without ever reading a tenant's data.

Tenants and projects: your role in each, and each tenant's trust tier.

Usage: metered cost per run, by token and resource class, against every quota.

Your data: a GDPR export, and a deletion that purges every store.

Administration · Deploy on your laptop or Google Cloud · Roadmap: what comes next

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Each use case below is a Guided template, so an analyst can start it from a spreadsheet, and a built-in model that a data scientist can configure, extend or replace in a spec. All four share the platform: sandboxed runs, the scorecard, endpoints, snippets, webhooks and embeds.

Use case Guided template Model The question it answers Budget planning Geo marketing mix mmm.hierarchical_geo (or mmm.pymc_marketing, mmm.bayesinsight) What does each channel bring in, and where should the next euro go? Weekly forecasting Weekly forecast ts.hsgp_trend What will this series do over the next weeks, and how sure are we? Store demand Demand by store tabular.regressor (xgboost, quantiles) How much will each store sell, including a store that opens next month? Customer choice Customer choice choice.multinomial_logit Which product does a shopper pick, and how does a price change shift that?

docs.title: Marketing-mix budget planning with Atlas
docs.text:
The question. Media spend goes to TV, search and social in several markets. What did each channel add to revenue, what is each euro returning now, and how should next quarter's budget be split?

The data. One row per week and market: revenue, spend per channel, and optional controls such as price or distribution. Two years of weekly data is a good start. MFF long tables (BayesInsight), Meridian-shaped tables and BayesInsight projects are recognised directly.

What you get.

  • Contribution and ROI per channel and market with 90% ranges, response curves and a decomposition of revenue into baseline and channels.
  • Beliefs entered as ROI or share ranges and lift tests as calibration, translated into model priors in a sandbox with a preview in business units.
  • What-if sliders whose ranges stay joint when several channels move, "Run exact", channel-off counterfactuals and forecasts.
  • An endpoint that a planning tool calls, and an Atlas RemoteModel that optimises allocations against it. On a laptop, Atlas found +0.22 % revenue at the same budget by moving spend from TV to search (measured).

Start here. Your first MMM in Guided mode → Priors, lift tests and the scorecard → Optimise a budget with Atlas. Coming from BayesInsight: import a BayesInsight model. Writing your own MMM: the marketing-mix guide.

docs.title: Weekly forecasting
docs.text:
The question. Orders, visits, calls or sales: what will the next 8 to 26 weeks look like, with a range a planner can use?

The data. One date column and one numeric column, weekly or daily, with at least two seasons of history for a seasonal pattern.

What you get.

  • A forecast fan: the median and the 50% and 90% ranges, with the fitted history and the split line, so you can see how the model did on the weeks it did not see.
  • A holdout check: the error and how often the actual values fell inside the 90% range.
  • The model's max_extension declares how far it may forecast; a longer horizon is refused with HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT before any compute.
  • A Google Sheet that refreshes the forecast every morning from the endpoint.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Weekly forecast) → Connect Google Sheets → Forecasting and sequential models.

docs.title: Demand by store
docs.text:
The question. How many units will each store sell each week, given prices, promotions and the calendar, and what about a store the model has never seen?

The data. One row per store and week: units sold, and drivers such as price and a promotion flag.

What you get.

  • An xgboost model with calendar features, a low and a high estimate (quantiles) per store and week, and the importance of each driver.
  • New stores scored by declaration: the store dim's policy says whether an unseen store may be scored and how, instead of whatever the model does with an unknown category.
  • An endpoint a replenishment system can call with next week's plan, and a webhook when a refit is ready.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Demand by store) → Tabular models → Endpoints and webhooks → Receive webhooks. The xgb_store_demand conformance fixture runs the same problem end to end in a few seconds.

docs.title: Customer choice
docs.text:
The question. On each shopping trip, which product does a household pick, and how does a price change or a promotion shift the shares?

The data. One row per trip and product: which product was chosen, its price and any promotion, with the household and the trip identified.

What you get.

  • A conditional logit with household effects and Bayesian-bootstrap draws.
  • The holdout hit rate on each household's last trip, compared with always guessing the most popular product, in plain words on the scorecard.
  • Price and promotion counterfactuals: how the shares move when a price changes.

Start here. The Guided tutorial (pick Customer choice) → Built-in models.

docs.title: Your own model
docs.text: None of the four fits? A PyMC model is one build() method and an sklearn model one estimator(); the platform handles the coordinates, splits, replayed preprocessing, summaries, bundles, endpoints and integrations. Port a model in 15 minutes · Why modeling-api?

docs.title: Why modeling-api?
docs.text: Most statistical models that matter to a business are built in a notebook, explained in a slide deck and then stop. Getting them in front of the people who make decisions, keeping them honest after the data changes, and letting other tools use them takes a second project that is mostly plumbing. modeling-api is that second project, done once, for a specific kind of model: Bayesian and classical models of labelled, multi-dimensional data (panels, time series, hierarchies) whose preprocessing and uncertainty must survive the trip to production.

docs.title: The problems it solves
docs.text: The problem What usually happens What modeling-api does The preprocessing at score time is not the preprocessing at fit time The scaling, lags and currency conversion are rewritten in the service, or refitted on the new data, or forgotten Steps store what they learned at fit time and replay it at score time, including per-group look-back tails; inverse transforms bring answers back to your units (Pipelines) Data is positional Column 7 changes meaning, a new market is "row 12", a forecast's lags start from the wrong week Data is an xr.Dataset with named dims; each dim declares what may happen at score time (fixed, extend, new_levels) and requests are checked against it before any compute (Labelled data) Uncertainty is dropped or summed wrongly A point estimate drives a budget decision; someone adds up 90% quantiles of 40 stores Every output carries its representation (draws, quantiles, interval, point, moments) and only the valid summaries and aggregations are offered (Representations) Every scenario needs the data scientist The analyst asks "what if we move 20% to search?" and waits a week Guided mode: templates, beliefs in business terms, a plain-language report and instant what-if sliders over per-draw response curves (Guided mode) Nobody knows whether to trust the model Convergence warnings in a log nobody reads A sanity scorecard (convergence, holdout error and coverage, plausibility, data) in plain words, and a promotion gate that uses it (Scorecard) Other tools need the model A Flask app per model, a shared pickle, a CSV emailed every Monday Endpoints with aliases, history and rollback, scoped tokens, generated snippets, signed webhooks, embeddable charts (Integrations) Many teams, untrusted code and data One shared server where anything can read anything Tenants with row-level security, a fresh sandbox per run, outputs verified against the storage's own checksums and signed, quotas and a kill switch (Security model)

docs.title: Compared with notebooks and an ad-hoc Flask app
docs.text:
The most common alternative, and a perfectly good one for a single model and a single team.

Notebook + a small web app modeling-api Getting started Minutes: you already have the notebook A spec or a build() method; Guided templates need no code at all Freedom Any library, any code Any PyMC or scikit-learn model through the plugin contract; built-in models for MMM, forecasting, demand and choice. Your own plugins run today on a deployment you control (installed into its runner); uploading them to a shared deployment comes in v0.5, first for allow-listed teams Preprocessing at score time Copied into the app by hand, or pickled with the model Declared steps with fitted state, replayed exactly; checked statically for leakage Forecasts and new groups Whatever the code does with an unseen row or date Declared per dim, checked before compute, with typed errors (UNSEEN_LEVELS, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT, …) Model versions File names, a model registry if you set one up Immutable spec revisions, signed bundles, lineage, endpoints with history and rollback Who can use it People who can run the notebook or call the app Analysts in Guided mode, other apps through endpoints, sheets, BI embeds, webhooks Security Whatever the app does; often pickle and an open port Sign-in, roles, scoped tokens, sandboxed runs, no pickle, verified outputs Operating it You own the server You own the deployment (a laptop, Docker Compose or Google Cloud); multi-tenant from the start

Stay with the notebook when the model is a one-off analysis nobody else needs to call. Move when a second person, a second model or a second application needs it.

docs.title: Compared with marketing-mix vendors and libraries
docs.text:
Marketing-mix modelling is the first domain pack, so this comparison comes up most. modeling-api is not a new MMM methodology and does not compete with the statistics of the established libraries; it is a platform that runs MMMs and puts them in front of planners.

Open-source MMM libraries (such as PyMC-Marketing, Google's Meridian, Meta's Robyn) are excellent at the model. They are libraries: you run them in a notebook, and serving, scenario tools for analysts, versioning and access control are up to you.

  • PyMC-Marketing models run on the platform through the mmm.pymc_marketing adapter, with business priors translated into its own model_config (MMM guide).
  • Meridian-shaped tables (time, geo, kpi, <channel>_spend) are recognised by the ingest; the Meridian model itself is not shipped (it needs TensorFlow).
  • BayesInsight's model_def.json runs as a built-in model or maps onto the geo MMM (import tutorial).
  • Robyn (R) is not supported.

Managed MMM services typically bundle data collection from ad platforms, a methodology, modelling as a service and planning dashboards. modeling-api does not collect data from ad platforms and offers no consulting; in exchange you own the spec, the data and the fitted posterior, can read every prior and every check, run models other than MMM on the same platform, and connect the result to your own tools.

Typical managed MMM service Open-source MMM library modeling-api Data collection from ad platforms Often included No No: upload CSV, Parquet, MFF or Meridian-shaped tables The model The vendor's Yours, in code A built-in hierarchical geo MMM, the PyMC-Marketing adapter, BayesInsight's model, or your own plugin Priors and calibration Varies, often hidden Yours, in code Business priors as ROI or share ranges, lift tests, all visible in the spec Analyst scenarios Dashboards You build them What-if sliders with joint uncertainty, "Run exact", forecasts and counterfactuals Budget optimisation Usually included Library functions Atlas against an endpoint today; an in-sandbox optimize job in v0.5 Other models on the same platform No No Forecasting, store demand, customer choice, your own Who owns the posterior The vendor You You

docs.title: Compared with generic ML model serving
docs.text:
MLflow, BentoML, KServe, Seldon and the cloud providers' endpoints are excellent at what they target: packaging a trained model from almost any framework and serving it with low latency and autoscaling. modeling-api targets a narrower problem and makes different trade-offs.

Generic model serving modeling-api Input contract Column or tensor signatures: names and shapes, no dimensions xr.Dataset with named dims, coordinates, roles, units and per-dim score policies Preprocessing at score time Up to you: bundle it into the artifact, or re-implement it Declared steps with fitted state, replayed exactly; stage-aware splits and per-group context tails New groups and horizons Whatever the model does with an unseen row Declared per dim (fixed, extend, new_levels + strategy); checked before compute Uncertainty Point predictions by default; intervals are a custom output A first-class representation that decides which summaries and aggregations are valid Units of the answer Whatever space the model was trained in Inverted to original units, with the output space recorded on every variable Serialization Framework-native; pickle and cloudpickle are common Zarr zip + JSON, skops or xgboost JSON; pickle is rejected on write and on read Promotion Usually manual, or a CI job Gated on a sanity scorecard; overrides need an admin's audited reason Latency Milliseconds, warm replicas, autoscaling, GPUs Batch: one sandboxed run per call (seconds, plus cold start in the cloud), and instant what-if from precomputed grids. No GPUs, no warm scorers yet Frameworks Almost any PyMC, scikit-learn, xgboost and hand-written models through the plugin contract Who it is for ML engineers serving many model types Statisticians, data scientists and the analysts and apps that use their models

docs.title: When to use something else
docs.text:
• You need sub-second answers from the exact model, or thousands of requests per second: use a model server. modeling-api answers sliders instantly from precomputed grids, but an exact score is a sandboxed run.
  • Deep learning or GPU work: not supported before the scale milestone.
  • Arbitrary workflows or DAGs: v1 pipelines are linear, and there is no general orchestration.
  • Your model needs the network at run time (an API, a database): runs have no egress by design.
  • You want hosted public code upload today: on a shared deployment, uploaded plugins come first to allow-listed teams (v0.5) and to the public only after an external penetration test. On a deployment you control you can install and run your own plugins now.

docs.title: Where it stands
docs.text: v0.4 is complete and tested on a laptop: the whole M3 journey passes end to end against a live stack, and the numbers on the home page come from those runs. Two things are honestly still open: the cloud controls are tested against fakes until they meet a real Google Cloud project, and the study with five non-technical testers is still to run. See M3 verification and the roadmap.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
modeling-api is built from a few ideas that fit together. Each page in this section explains one of them with code you can run.

flowchart TB
    subgraph CP["Contracts — mapi-spec (pure JSON, no numpy)"]
        direction LR
        SCH["DataSchema<br/>dims · policies · roles"]
        SPEC["ModelSpec<br/>pipeline · model · split"]
        REQ["ScoreRequest<br/>mode · horizon · output"]
        CAT["Catalog<br/>settings schemas · schema effects · manifests"]
        VAL["Static validation<br/>stages · leakage · CoordPlan"]
    end
    subgraph RT["Runtime — mapi-sdk (xarray)"]
        direction LR
        PIPE["Pipeline<br/>fit → state · transform · inverse"]
        PLUG["Model plugin<br/>fit · score"]
        COORD["Coord canonicalisation"]
        SUM["Summariser<br/>representation-aware"]
        BUN[("Bundle")]
    end
    SPEC --> VAL
    SCH --> VAL
    CAT --> VAL
    REQ --> VAL
    VAL -->|"resolved spec"| PIPE
    PIPE --> PLUG --> BUN
    BUN --> COORD --> PLUG
    PLUG --> SUM

The split between the two halves matters. The contracts are JSON in, JSON out; the platform's API depends only on them, so it can validate any spec and any score request without importing your code or decoding your arrays. The runtime touches arrays and runs plugins; it lives in notebooks and in the sandboxed runner. How the platform puts the two halves together is in the Architecture overview, and what keeps it safe in the Security model.

docs.title: The ideas
docs.text:
• Labelled data

    Data is an xr.Dataset. A DataSchema gives each dim a policy (fixed, extend, new_levels) and each variable a role, units and missingness rules. Bindings map your names to a model's canonical names and back.

  • Pipelines and stages

    Steps learn state on train and replay it at score time. The split happens at a named stage; look-back steps store per-group context tails; inverse transforms stop at the last reshape and record the output space.

  • Representations and summaries

    Draws, quantiles, intervals, points and moments. The representation decides which summaries exist and which aggregations are honest.

  • Bundles

    The fitted artifact: one zarr zip plus JSON sidecars, every file hashed, no pickle.

  • Coord plans and typed errors

    Score requests are checked against the fitted coordinates before any compute: unseen levels, horizons, gaps, missing future covariates, impossible summaries.

  • Capabilities and manifests

    What a model declares about itself, statically: representation, score modes, outputs, derived quantities, which preprocessing it owns.

  • Tenancy and authentication v0.3

    Tenants, projects and roles; API tokens and their scopes; browser sign-in; how every request is authorized.

  • Quotas and cost v0.3

    vCPU-second quotas at token, tenant and global level; interactive and batch priority; exact per-run cost from a versioned price table.

  • Guided mode v0.4

    Templates, plain-language questions with role detection, business priors and lift tests, the sanity scorecard and instant what-if sliders over per-draw response grids.

  • Integrations v0.4

    Endpoints and aliases with a gated promotion, code snippets, signed webhooks, rendered and embedded plots, and the trust lifecycle from sign-up to deletion.

docs.title: Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Canonical name The name a step or model uses (geo, time, y). data.bind maps it to your dataset's name (market, date, revenue). Stage The dataset after a named step. raw is the bound input. Splits, context and scenario entry points (inputs_stage) all refer to stages. Step state What a step learned at fit time: JSON plus labelled arrays (for example scale(geo, channel)), and a context tail for look-back steps. Never written into the spec. Score The umbrella term for "predict with replayed preprocessing". Modes: predict, forecast, counterfactual, simulate, filter, evaluate. Representation How a model encodes uncertainty: draws, quantiles, interval, point or moments. Output space Where an output's values live after inversion, for example raw or weekly. Bundle The verified result of a fit: states, model groups, native artifacts, manifest and hashes. Run A unit of work (fit, score, …) submitted to an executor as JSON.

docs.title: Architecture overview v0.4
docs.text:
modeling-api is three layers, built in this order: a typed modelling runtime (the SDK, the steps and the model plugins), a job platform around it (the API, the queue, the executors and the runner), and, from v0.3, a hosted multi-tenant platform. The rules that make the last one safe hold from the first: the control plane never imports plugin code and never decodes your arrays, every run happens in a sandbox, and every output is checked against what the storage itself computed.

flowchart TB
    subgraph clients["Clients"]
        web["Web app<br/>(app origin)"]
        sandbox["Plot sandbox<br/>(separate origin)"]
        cli["mapi CLI · Python client ·<br/>curl · other apps"]
    end
    subgraph control["Control plane: JSON only, never imports plugins"]
        api["API<br/>/v1 · OpenAPI · SSE"]
        orch["Orchestrator<br/>dispatcher · reconciler ·<br/>finalizer · event ingestion"]
        pg[("PostgreSQL<br/>runs · queue · events ·<br/>registry · catalog")]
    end
    subgraph exec["Run sandbox: one per run"]
        sup["Supervisor<br/>(trusted, holds the run's URLs)"]
        wrk["Worker<br/>(untrusted: SDK + plugin)"]
    end
    store[("Object store<br/>quarantine · bootstrap · runs ·<br/>bundles · data")]

    web -->|"/v1"| api
    cli -->|"/v1"| api
    web -. "postMessage<br/>(validated)" .-> sandbox
    web -->|"signed PUT / GET"| store
    api --> pg
    orch --> pg
    api -->|"metadata, signed URLs"| store
    orch -->|"bootstrap object,<br/>verify, server-side copy"| store
    orch -->|"submit(run id, nonce)"| sup
    sup <-->|"socketpair"| wrk
    sup -->|"signed URLs only"| store
    sup -->|"HMAC-signed events"| orch

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Component Package What it does What it never does API mapi-server (mapi-server api) The /v1 HTTP API: datasets, specs and their static validation, runs, models, scoring, plots; server-sent events; signed URLs Import mapi_sdk, a plugin, numpy or xarray (an import-linter contract, also enforced inside the server image) Orchestrator mapi-server (mapi-server worker) Dispatcher, reconciler, event ingestion and the finalizer, over a procrastinate queue in the same PostgreSQL Decode a dataset or a bundle: it reads object metadata and size-capped JSON sidecars only Executor mapi_server.executors Starts a runner for a run: local-process (a subprocess), docker / docker-gvisor (a container); Cloud Run Jobs in v0.3 Pass anything but the run id and a nonce Runner mapi-runner A trusted supervisor that fetches the run's instructions, starts an untrusted worker, uploads outputs and signs events Let the worker touch credentials, the network of the store or its stdout SDK and plugins mapi-sdk, mapi-steps, mapi-pymc, mapi-sklearn, mapi-plugin-* The modelling runtime: pipelines with fitted state, models, coord plans, summaries, bundles Run anywhere but in the worker (on the platform) or your own process (as a library) Contracts mapi-spec Every shape both sides agree on: specs, schemas, DTOs, the run protocol, error codes Import numpy, xarray or pandas Object store mapi-gcs-shim locally, Cloud Storage later Buckets with object generations, server-computed CRC32C and MD5, signed URLs and POST policies, per-principal permissions — Web app, plot sandbox apps/web, apps/plot-sandbox The Guided and Expert UI and the Integrations hub; the plot sandbox is the only place Vega-Lite and Plotly specs render, including shared embed pages Render a plot on the app's own origin

docs.title: The control plane
docs.text:
The API and the orchestrator share one PostgreSQL database. The API writes runs in state created and decides queued or rejected from static checks; everything after that belongs to the orchestrator.

flowchart LR
    subgraph api["API process"]
        routes["/v1 routes"]
        validate["Static validation<br/>(SchemaEffect JSON,<br/>CoordPlan, sanitizers)"]
        sse["SSE fan-out<br/>(one LISTEN per process)"]
    end
    subgraph worker["Worker process"]
        disp["Dispatcher<br/>token bucket · intent row"]
        rec["Reconciler<br/>every 10 s"]
        ev["Event ingestion<br/>HMAC verify · dedupe"]
        fin["Finalizer<br/>(procrastinate job)"]
    end
    pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    routes --> validate
    routes -->|"runs, specs,<br/>datasets"| pg
    disp -->|"lease queued runs"| pg
    rec -->|"executor status →<br/>state transitions"| pg
    ev -->|"run_progress upsert,<br/>run_events + NOTIFY"| pg
    fin -->|"model versions,<br/>signed manifests"| pg
    pg -->|"NOTIFY"| sse
  • Static validation runs in the API, synchronously, from JSON only: each step's exported schema effect and each model's settings schema and schema template, taken from the catalog. The catalog is produced by a sandboxed describe run of the real runner and cached per image digest, so the API validates against exactly what the runner will execute.
  • The dispatcher leases queued runs through a token bucket, writes an intent row (run, attempt, nonce) and then calls the executor, so a crash between the two can be recovered.
  • The reconciler is level-triggered: every 10 seconds it compares each active run with the executor's own status, which is the source of truth for liveness. Silence only marks a run stalled; an execution that vanished is retried as a new attempt (within a cost window), and orphaned executions are adopted by their nonce.
  • The finalizer turns a finished execution into a model version (see Storage and integrity).
  • Events are verified, deduplicated on (run, attempt, seq), and stored as one run_progress row per run plus run_events for state changes, warnings, diagnostics and metrics. A PostgreSQL NOTIFY wakes the SSE streams of every API process.

The state machine, every transition and who owns it are in the Run protocol.

docs.title: The run sandbox
docs.text:
Every run, whatever its kind (ingest, describe, validate, fit, score), gets a fresh pair of processes: a trusted supervisor and an untrusted worker.

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Dispatcher
    participant S as Object store
    participant X as Executor
    participant R as Supervisor
    participant W as Worker (SDK + plugin)
    D->>S: PUT bootstrap/{nonce}: RunSpec (signed URLs, HMAC key, limits)
    D->>X: submit(MAPI_RUN_ID, MAPI_NONCE)
    X->>R: start (no secrets in argv or env)
    R->>S: GET bootstrap/{nonce}, then DELETE it
    R->>S: GET inputs (signed, generation-pinned, CRC32C-checked)
    R->>W: spawn: scrubbed env, separate uid (where possible), python -I
    W-->>R: progress, logs, results (framed JSON over a socketpair)
    R-->>D: stdout: one HMAC-signed event per line
    R->>S: POST outputs (V4 POST policy on the attempt prefix)
    R->>S: PUT manifest.json (signed claim of every object)
    R-->>D: "complete" event, exit 0
  • No credentials in the environment. The executor passes only MAPI_RUN_ID and MAPI_NONCE. The run's signed URLs and its event HMAC key are in a one-time bootstrap object that the supervisor reads and deletes before any model code starts.
  • The worker is untrusted. It runs the SDK harness and the plugin with an allow-listed environment (every MAPI_* removed), in its own session, under uid 10001 with no_new_privs when the supervisor runs as root (containers, Cloud Run). It talks only to the supervisor, through length-prefixed JSON frames that must match their schemas.
  • Only the supervisor writes events. Its stdout carries one JSON event per line, each with a sequence number and an HMAC; anything the worker prints becomes a capped, control-character-stripped log event.
  • Caps everywhere. Log lines (4 KB) and total logs (20 MB), event size, output objects and bytes, and a scratch budget per resource class. Breaking one is a SANDBOX_VIOLATION or RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, never a silent truncation of results.
  • Checkpoints. On SIGTERM or near the deadline, a PyMC fit flushes its last segment and the supervisor uploads a partial manifest; the run can be resumed from there.

On a laptop the worker cannot change user, so runs report DEV_MODE_ISOLATION: the process split, the scrubbed environment, the event signing and the output verification all still apply, but the worker runs as you. See the security model.

docs.title: Storage and integrity
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph buckets["Buckets: mapi-{env}-*"]
        q["quarantine<br/>uploads, 7-day lifecycle"]
        b["bootstrap<br/>one-time RunSpecs"]
        r["runs<br/>attempt scratch"]
        bun["bundles<br/>write-once, retention lock"]
        d["data<br/>content-addressed datasets"]
    end
    browser(("browser /<br/>client")) -->|"signed PUT"| q
    q -->|"signed GET"| ingest["ingest run"]
    ingest -->|"POST policy"| r
    r -->|"verify, then<br/>server-side copy"| d
    fit["fit / score run"] -->|"POST policy"| r
    r -->|"verify, then<br/>server-side copy"| bun
    bun -->|"signed GET, minted after<br/>the manifest signature checks"| client(("client"))
Bucket Who writes Who reads quarantine Browsers and clients, through a signed PUT for one object Ingest runs, through a signed GET bootstrap The dispatcher The supervisor, with a principal that may get and delete there and nothing else (no list) runs Runs, through a POST policy limited to their attempt prefix and a size range The finalizer (metadata) bundles The finalizer only, by server-side copy; write-once under a retention lock Clients and runs, through signed GETs minted after verification data The finalizer, by server-side copy of ingest outputs Runs, through signed GETs

Outputs are claims. When a run ends, the finalizer lists the attempt prefix and reads each object's metadata: the size, CRC32C, MD5 and generation the store computed. It compares them with the run's signed manifest and refuses missing, changed or unexpected objects (INTEGRITY_FAILURE). It validates the small JSON sidecars under size caps, sanitizes the plots, copies the verified generations into the bundles bucket, and signs a bundle manifest that binds the tenant, run, spec hash, data hash, catalog digest and every destination generation (an EC P-256 key locally, standing in for Cloud KMS). Every later download link is minted only after that signature checks, so a swapped object can never be served. Bundles themselves are zarr zips plus JSON: nothing is pickled.

docs.title: The event path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["Worker"] -->|"frames"| S["Supervisor"]
    S -->|"stdout:<br/>{mapi_event, hmac}"| P{{"local executor:<br/>stdout pipe"}}
    S -.->|"v0.3: Cloud Logging<br/>→ Pub/Sub push"| I["POST /internal/events"]
    P --> V["Verify HMAC ·<br/>dedupe (run, attempt, seq)"]
    I --> V
    V -->|"progress: upsert"| RP[("run_progress")]
    V -->|"state, warning, diagnostic,<br/>metric, complete, error"| RE[("run_events")]
    RE -->|"NOTIFY"| SSE["SSE streams<br/>Last-Event-ID resume"]
    RP --> SSE
    SSE --> C(("web app ·<br/>CLI · client"))

Locally the executor reads events straight from the supervisor's stdout. In the cloud the same lines travel through Cloud Logging and Pub/Sub to POST /internal/events; the verification is the same. Progress is coalesced to one event every couple of seconds and kept as a single row, so a long fit does not write thousands of rows; only state changes, warnings, diagnostics, checkpoints, metrics and terminal events are persisted and replayed to a reconnecting client.

docs.title: The integration paths (v0.4)
docs.text:
Three paths take a model's results out of the platform. None of them gives the outside world more than it needs: an endpoint call runs in a sandbox like any score, a webhook carries ids and states only, and an embed link shows one chart.

flowchart LR
    subgraph out["Outside"]
        app["Sheets · BI · Atlas ·<br/>your app"]
        rcv["Your webhook<br/>receiver"]
        viewer["A viewer's browser<br/>(Notion, Looker Studio, …)"]
    end
    subgraph cp["Control plane"]
        ep["POST /v1/endpoints/{alias}/score<br/>score:<alias> token · input contract ·<br/>CoordPlan · rate limit and budget"]
        outbox[("events outbox<br/>written in the same<br/>transaction as the change")]
        relay["Worker relay<br/>retries · SSRF guard ·<br/>HMAC signature"]
        embed["GET /v1/embeds/{token}<br/>no credentials ·<br/>one platform-recipe plot"]
    end
    sb["Score run<br/>(fresh sandbox)"]
    bun[("Verified bundles")]
    page["Plot sandbox origin<br/>/embed/<token>"]

    app -->|"inline XrJSON"| ep --> sb --> bun
    ep -->|"signed links to the outputs"| app
    sb -. "score.completed" .-> outbox
    outbox --> relay -->|"Mapi-Signature"| rcv
    viewer --> page -->|"fetch, CSP-limited"| embed
    embed -->|"data inlined from the<br/>verified bundle"| bun
  • Endpoints freeze the model version's input contract when it is promoted, so a call is checked statically (dims, coordinates, future covariates) before a run is started; the payload is stored as a run input and decoded only in the sandbox. Promotion goes through the scorecard gate.
  • Webhooks are written to an outbox in the same transaction as the change they report (a finished run, a ready model version, a promotion), then delivered by the worker through the SSRF guard, signed, retried and logged.
  • Embeds are served to a page on the plot sandbox's origin, which may fetch nothing but the public embed view; the API inlines the plot's data from the verified bundle without decoding it (Sharing plots).

docs.title: Bundles
docs.text:
A bundle is everything a fit produced that scoring needs, in a form that is safe to store, move and read back: one bundle.zarr.zip plus four JSON sidecars.

fruit-demand-v1/
├── bundle.zarr.zip      # one zarr v3 zip: the whole fitted model as an xr.DataTree
├── manifest.json        # identity, provenance, lineage and the hashes of every file
├── metrics.json         # holdout metrics (computed through the score path)
├── diagnostics.json     # convergence and sanity checks, expert and plain-language
├── plots.json           # rendered, sanitized plots for outputs.plots
└── evaluation/          # evaluate_then_refit: the train-only bundle behind the metrics

docs.title: Write, read, verify
docs.text:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

from mapi_sdk import Bundle

out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "fruit-demand-v1"
manifest = bundle.write(out)
print(sorted(p.name for p in out.iterdir()))
# ['bundle.zarr.zip', 'diagnostics.json', 'evaluation', 'manifest.json', 'metrics.json',
#  'plots.json']  - `evaluation/` is the train-only fit that produced the holdout metrics

again = Bundle.read(out, registry)  # every file's size and hashes are verified here
assert again.bundle_id == bundle.bundle_id

Bundle.read recomputes the size, CRC32C, MD5 and SHA-256 of every file and compares them with the manifest. A damaged or tampered bundle raises BundleError (INTEGRITY_FAILURE).

docs.title: What is inside
docs.text:
print(manifest.role, manifest.plugin["id"], manifest.spec_hash[:19])
# production tabular.regressor sha256:...
print(manifest.files["bundle.zarr.zip"])  # size, crc32c, md5 (GCS forms) and sha256
print(manifest.lineage["evaluation_bundle"])  # the train-only fit behind the metrics

tree = again.to_tree()  # the whole bundle as one xr.DataTree
print(sorted(tree.children))
# ['binding', 'fit_coords', 'model', 'native', 'preprocess', 'schema', 'spec']
print(sorted(tree["preprocess"].children))  # ['cal', 'logy']: one node per step
Node Holds /spec The canonical spec and the resolved spec (pinned versions, every stage's schema) /schema/raw, /schema/model The data contract at the input and at the model stage /binding Canonical ↔ dataset names, reversed on every output /preprocess/<step> Each step's learned JSON state, labelled arrays and per-group context tail /model The manifest, settings, fit config and learned JSON /model/<group> ArviZ-named groups: posterior, sample_stats, log_likelihood, observed_data, … /terminal_state Sequential models: the filtered state at the last fitted step /native Safe native artifacts: skops files, xgboost JSON, … /derived/<name> Derived quantities cached at fit (contributions, response curves) /fit_coords/<stage> The fitted coordinates at every stage (what CoordPlan checks against) /side_tables/<name> pinned side tables, frozen with the fit /thin The bundle-wide thinning index for draws

docs.title: No pickle, ever
docs.text:
Pickle executes code when it is loaded, so it has no place in an artifact that moves between users, services and sandboxes.

  • Model groups are labelled arrays in zarr; settings, states and manifests are JSON.
  • Native estimators are stored as skops (loading lists the file's types first and refuses anything outside that estimator's allow-list) or xgboost JSON.
  • FitOutput.native entries that look like pickle (.pkl, .joblib, .pt, pickle magic bytes, …) are rejected when a bundle is written and when it is read. The contract kit checks it for every plugin.

docs.title: Hashes in the forms object stores report
docs.text: CRC32C and MD5 are recorded base64-encoded, the way Google Cloud Storage computes them on upload. The platform binds a signed manifest to the object generations and server-computed hashes, so an uploaded artifact cannot be swapped or replayed (see Storage and integrity). SHA-256 is recorded too, for content addressing.

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
The manifest records the spec hash, the data hash, the plugin and every step version, and the library versions a bundle was fitted with; manifest.lineage links a production bundle to its evaluation bundle. "Which data and which code made this forecast?" always has an answer.

Next: Coord plans and typed errors.

docs.title: Capabilities and manifests
docs.text:
A model plugin describes itself with a manifest: static JSON that says what data it needs, what it can do, what it returns and which settings it takes. The control plane validates specs and score requests against manifests, and the Guided UI builds its forms from them, all without ever importing the plugin.

from mapi_sdk import default_registry

registry = default_registry()
manifest = registry.model("mmm.hierarchical_geo@^1").manifest()
caps = manifest.capabilities

print(caps.representation.value, caps.inference)  # draws mcmc
print(sorted(caps.score_modes))
# ['counterfactual', 'evaluate', 'forecast', 'predict', 'simulate']
print(caps.decision, caps.contribution_scale)  # True additive
print([d.name for d in manifest.derived])  # ['contributions', 'response_curves', 'marginal_cost']

basic = [k for k, v in manifest.settings_schema["properties"].items() if v.get("x-ui-level") == "basic"]
print(basic)  # ['pooling', 'adstock', 'saturation']: what Guided mode shows

adapter = registry.model("mmm.pymc_marketing@^1").manifest().capabilities
print(sorted(adapter.owns))  # ['carryover', 'inverse_units', 'scaling']

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text: Field Meaning inference mcmc, vi, map, smc, kalman, point, bootstrap or custom representation draws, quantiles, interval, point or moments. See Representations score_modes Which of predict, forecast, counterfactual, simulate, filter, evaluate the model supports. Anything else is MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED decision Has an objective(fitted, decision) returning a value per draw, for budget optimisation recommend Can recommend candidates (Bayesian optimisation) fast_score Provides a compiled fast-scoring path (PyMC FrozenPredictor) contribution_scale additive (contributions sum to the prediction; the contract kit checks it), multiplicative or none loo_valid, loo_invalid_reason Whether pointwise LOO is meaningful. An HMM's steps are dependent, so ts.gaussian_hmm declares it invalid and elpd_loo is rejected at validation identified_quantities Which parameters are identified (for models with label switching or rotations) owns Preprocessing the model does itself: scaling, carryover, inverse_units, recursion. The platform steps aside and labels outputs accordingly deterministic_given_seed Whether the same seed gives the same fit (nutpie: no). The contract kit checks it when claimed checkpointable Long fits can be checkpointed and resumed

docs.title: The manifest
Steps have manifests too
docs.text:
Each step exports a catalog entry: its settings JSON Schema, kind, whether it is stateful or invertible, which settings name variables, dims and side tables, its context need, and a schema effect template. The runner images export the catalog when they are built, and the API validates specs against it. Browse it in the steps catalog.

python -m mapi_steps.catalog --splits > catalog.json   # what the control plane loads

docs.title: Browse the built-ins
docs.text:
• Models catalog: every installed model's capabilities, outputs, derived quantities and settings.
  • Plot recipes catalog.
  • Spec schema: every field of ModelSpec and ScoreRequest.

docs.title: Coord plans and typed errors
docs.text: Before a score request touches a model, its coordinates are checked against what the model was fitted on. The checks are called the CoordPlan, and almost all of them need only metadata: the fitted coordinates of every stage (stored in the bundle) and the request itself. That is why the API can reject a bad request in milliseconds, without starting a sandbox.

docs.title: The checks
docs.text:
Code HTTP Raised when What to do UNSEEN_LEVELS 422 A label of a fixed dim (or a new_levels dim with strategy error) was not in the fit Drop it, or declare the dim new_levels with a strategy and refit COORD_NOT_ALLOWED 422 An extend dim starts before the fitted range, or a label cannot exist Send labels inside or right after the fit NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION 422 New time labels leave a gap after the fitted range Send the missing periods (context tails need them) HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT 409 The forecast reaches past max_extension Refit with a larger max_extension MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE 422 A future_required variable is missing over the horizon Supply it in the payload CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED 422 The output asks for something the representation cannot give (summing quantiles, draws from a point model, an HDI from quantiles) Ask for a valid summary, or use a model with joint draws RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED 422 A target lag shorter than the horizon Use longer lags or a model that owns recursion MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED 422 The model does not declare the requested mode See the model's capabilities SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE 422 A side table does not cover the periods a step needs Supply a table that covers them

HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT is a 409, not a 422: the request is fine, the model is not ready for it. The fix is a refit, not a different request.

docs.title: Metadata only: what the API checks
docs.text:
from mapi_sdk import CoordPlan
from mapi_spec import load_score_request, validate_score_request

# What the API stores next to a model version: JSON only, no arrays, no plugin code.
meta = CoordPlan(load_score_request(FORECAST), bundle.resolved, bundle.fit_coords).metadata()
print(f"{len(meta.model_dump_json()) / 1024:.0f} KiB of metadata")

request = load_score_request(FORECAST + "output: {summary: [hdi_90], draws: 100}\n")
for issue in validate_score_request(request, meta):  # no data, no model: milliseconds
    print(issue.code, issue.pointer, "-", issue.message)
# MISSING_FUTURE_COVARIATE /data - forecasting needs future values of ['price', 'promo'] ...
# CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED /output/draws - draws were requested but the model's
#                                        representation is 'quantiles'
# CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED /output/summary/0 - summary 'hdi_90' cannot be computed from
#                                            'quantiles' output

Every problem is reported at once, each with a JSON pointer into the request. The metadata is a few kilobytes of JSON per model version; no arrays are decoded and no plugin code is imported.

docs.title: In the runtime: the same checks, then canonicalisation
docs.text:
score_bundle runs the same checks against the real payload (so it can also see which values are present), raises the most specific error, and keeps the remaining notices (for example "1 new level of store will use strategy pooled") in the output's issues attribute.

from mapi_spec import ErrorCode, MapiError


def try_score(request_yaml: str, payload: xr.Dataset) -> ErrorCode:
    try:
        score_bundle(bundle, request_yaml, payload, registry=registry)
    except MapiError as err:
        print(err.code, "-", err)
        return err.code
    raise AssertionError("expected a typed error")


FORECAST = """
apiVersion: mapi/v1
kind: ScoreRequest
model: endpoint://quickstart/fruit-demand
mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 4}
"""

# 1. a forecast without next month's promotions: promo is future_required
code_1 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.drop_vars("promo"))

# 2. quantiles are per cell, so "total over all stores" would be a made-up number
code_2 = try_score(FORECAST + "output: {aggregate: {over: [store]}}\n", plan)

# 3. a product outside the fitted range: sku is a fixed dim
code_3 = try_score(FORECAST, plan.assign_coords(sku=["apples", "kiwis"]))

Then it canonicalises the model-stage data, so a plugin never has to reason about request order or new labels:

  1. Reorder every fixed and new_levels dim to the fit order. Posterior arrays are indexed by position, so county_03 must sit where it sat at fit time.
  2. Pad requested subsets out to the full fitted set (masked), so shapes match the fit.
  3. Append new levels after the fitted ones, flagged by a boolean coordinate <dim>__is_new; <dim>__requested marks real (non-padding) labels.
  4. Call plugin.score(...).
  5. Select the requested labels back, in request order, and drop the helper coordinates.
flowchart LR
    R["request: county_07, county_02, county_new"] --> O["fit order<br/>county_00 … county_07"]
    O --> P["+ county_new<br/>county__is_new = True"]
    P --> S["plugin.score"]
    S --> B["select back:<br/>county_07, county_02, county_new"]

Inside a plugin, mapi_sdk.new_level_mask(ds, "county") returns the __is_new flags and ScoreContext.strategy("county") the effective new-level strategy. PyMC models get all of this for free through ctx.hier_effect(...); see Bring a PyMC model.

docs.title: Errors are values, not strings
docs.text:
Every error is a MapiError with:

  • a stable code (an ErrorCode) and an HTTP status;
  • a platform-written detail, and the list of issues behind it, each of which can carry a suggested_action;
  • a JSON pointer to the offending field;
  • untrusted_text: anything a dataset or plugin said, kept apart from the message so a UI can render it as plain text and an agent can treat it as data, never as instructions.

Over HTTP an error is an RFC 7807 problem document. The full list is in Error codes.

Next: Capabilities and manifests.

docs.title: Guided mode v0.4
docs.text:
Guided mode is for analysts who know their business but not PyMC. It is organised around tasks, not screens: pick what you want to learn, answer questions about your columns, state what you already believe, run, read a plain-language report and play with what-if sliders. Behind every answer sits the same ModelSpec that Expert mode edits, so "View as YAML" always shows the real thing and Expert edits round-trip back.

This page explains the concepts and the contracts in mapi_spec that the server, the web app and the client share. The endpoints are listed in the HTTP API reference.

Status

The server and the runner serve every contract on this page: the data path (templates, role detection, drafts, the sandboxed ingest presets, the BayesInsight import and the persona lock, walked through in From a spreadsheet to a Guided draft) and the modelling path (business priors, lift tests, the scorecard, the what-if grids and the forecast and counterfactual views, in Guided modelling). The web app's Guided screens use all of it: see Your first analysis in Guided mode.

docs.title: The persona lock
docs.text:
Every user picks Guided or Expert in the header, and the choice is remembered (until then, a self-service workspace starts in Guided mode and any other in Expert). A project admin can lock a project to Guided mode (Project.guided_locked: Settings > Mode > Lock … to Guided mode in the web app, or PATCH /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/projects/{project_id}; audited as project.guided_lock): members below admin then only see Guided screens.

The API holds those members to the same line when they write specs (mapi_spec.guided.guided_lock_issues): a stored spec must be a Guided spec - its metadata.labels.guided names a template and model.use is that template's plugin - and the fields the template marks advanced or hidden keep their values (a revision keeps its parent's, a new spec the template's). Answers, basic settings, business priors and lift tests stay editable. Anything else is 403 FORBIDDEN with one issue per JSON pointer. Admins, static validation, runs and scoring - and so integrations calling endpoints - are not affected.

docs.title: 1. "What do you want to learn?" - templates
docs.text:
A template (GuidedTemplate) is data: a title and description in plain words, the questions, the built-in plugin it uses, a ModelSpec template with {{placeholder}} strings, default settings, the scorecard checks that apply and x-ui-level hints for every field.

Template Plugin For What-if Forecast Business priors geo_mmm - Geo marketing mix mmm.hierarchical_geo What each channel adds in each market; moving budget yes yes yes, and lift tests weekly_forecast - Weekly forecast ts.hsgp_trend One series, weeks or months ahead, with a range — yes — store_demand - Demand by store tabular.regressor Units per store and week from prices and promotions (low/median/high) — yes — customer_choice - Customer choice choice.multinomial_logit Which product customers pick and how price shifts the choice presets — —

Customer choice: a conditional logit with household effects

customer_choice targets the built-in choice.multinomial_logit: alternative-specific utilities over price and promotion, household-specific product preferences (a random-intercept logit fitted at its posterior mode) and Bayesian-bootstrap draws over households, so shares, counterfactual deltas and sums over trips keep their uncertainty. A product without a price on a trip was not on the shelf; new households draw their preferences from the fitted spread. Choice values must name products the way the price columns do (price_cola goes with the choice cola). See Built-in models.

Every template fits with fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit: the model is first fitted without the latest periods to measure its forecast error, then refitted on everything, which is what endpoints require.

docs.title: 2. Questions instead of a role mapper
docs.text:
Instead of mapping columns to dims and roles, the user answers questions such as "Which column is the result you want to explain?" or "Which columns are media spend (one per channel)?". A question (GuidedQuestion) says what its answer becomes:

  • a dim (date → the time dim, geo → markets), with the dim's policy;
  • a variable with a role (kpi → the target);
  • one variable along a new dim built from several columns (spend → one spend variable along channel, one label per column: tv_spend becomes channel tv);
  • several separate variables (controls), or a choice or a number (frequency, holdout length).

docs.title: Role detection
docs.text:
The browser profiles the upload locally (nothing hostile reaches the servers just to be previewed) and sends ColumnProfiles - name, type, row and missing counts, distinct values, range, detected date frequency. POST /v1/guided/detect-roles (or the pure function mapi_spec.guided.suggest_roles) ranks the columns for every question and pre-fills answers:

  • names are split into words (SearchSpend → search spend) and matched against each question's keywords;
  • types must fit (a date question wants dates; spend wants numbers, preferably never negative);

  • label-like columns (few repeated values) suit dim questions; mostly empty columns lose points.

  • dates in order and trip numbers that count up suit ordered dims; spend with negative values and columns that never change lose points.

Every candidate comes with a confidence between 0 and 1 and a reason_plain such as "named like a revenue column; never negative". Answers are pre-filled at confidence 0.5 or more, a column answers at most one question, and the data frequency is read from the chosen date column. Required questions left without a candidate come back as warnings.

Detection also works on a stored dataset version (dataset instead of columns): its ingest run wrote columns.json, the sandbox's profile of every uploaded column (for MFF uploads: of the pivoted variables), and versions without one are profiled from their stored schema and summary - the API only ever reads that JSON.

docs.title: Drafts and "View as YAML"
docs.text:
POST /v1/guided/drafts (mapi_spec.guided.build_draft) turns GuidedAnswers into a GuidedDraft:

  • an IngestMapping for the upload (column names become safe dataset names: Revenue (EUR) → revenue_eur);
  • the ModelSpec document, with every placeholder filled from answers, template defaults or lookups (for example the season length from the frequency), and the business priors and lift tests in its calibration block;
  • the same spec as YAML.

The server validates the draft statically against the catalog, with the schema the mapping promises (mapi_spec.guided.draft_schema), and returns the findings in issues. Nothing is stored: upload the data as a dataset version with the mapping and save the spec with POST /v1/specs. Wrong answers come back as GUIDED_ANSWERS_INVALID pointing at /answers/<question>.

docs.title: File formats and presets
docs.text:
Uploads are parsed only in a sandboxed ingest run. Besides an explicit column mapping, the IngestMapping.preset field names a file contract marketing teams already have:

Format or preset Contract csv, parquet A column mapping: dims, vars and, for wide tables, wide (WideVarMapping: one variable from one column per label) mff (format or preset) The MFF long table below meridian Google Meridian's CoordToColumns wide table (MeridianColumns): time, geo, kpi, controls, and parallel media/media_spend (and reach/frequency) lists per channel bayesinsight An MFF table plus BayesInsight's metadata.json (BayesInsightMetadata) zarr_zip, netcdf Self-describing labelled datasets

The MFF ("model feature format") long table has one row per period, key combination and variable - the columns BayesInsight uses (mapi_spec.ingest.MFF_COLUMNS):

Column Meaning Period The date; weekly data must fall on the same weekday Geography, Product, Outlet, Campaign, Creative Key columns; each becomes a dim when it has more than one value VariableName The variable (Sales, TV_Spend, ...) VariableValue The value

MFF tables can also be pivoted and then mapped like a CSV (the variables become columns), MffOptions.combine joins key columns into one dim, and the BayesInsight preset keeps only what metadata.json allows. The ingest enforces caps on rows, columns, cell length and decompression and explains every refusal; see File formats and presets.

docs.title: BayesInsight models
docs.text:
A BayesInsight project imports as a draft (POST /v1/guided/import/bayesinsight, mapi_spec.bayesinsight.import_bayesinsight) for the built-in geo MMM mmm.hierarchical_geo (Q8): the data with the bayesinsight preset - media variables gathered into spend along channel, the row_ids key columns joined into one geo dim - and a spec that carries every feature with an equivalent (delayed or geometric adstock and its Beta/Exponential priors per channel, Hill saturation, pooling, standardised controls, Fourier seasonality). Features without one - non-Normal likelihoods, coefficient priors in KPI units, Weibull adstock, S-shaped curves, sign constraints - are listed as IMPORT_UNSUPPORTED warnings; models that cannot run (no single exog KPI, no media, names that do not match row_ids) are refused with IMPORT_UNSUPPORTED.

target: mmm.bayesinsight imports for the dedicated built-in mmm.bayesinsight, which runs BayesInsight's model as model_def.json defines it: its likelihoods (Normal, log-normal, Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated), coefficient and intercept priors in the KPI's own units, Hill, linear and S-shaped curves before delayed, geometric or Weibull carry-over, enforced sign constraints, fixed and partially pooled effects per row id, Fourier seasons and local spline trends. Every row id becomes a panel dim of its own, variables keep their MFF names, and the draft is validated against the catalog like any other. What the plugin cannot run (an MvNormal likelihood, time transforms, unknown prior families) falls back to BayesInsight's default with an IMPORT_UNSUPPORTED warning; faithful but surprising behaviour (no likelihood means Poisson, random effects with partial_pooling_sigma: 0 pool nothing) is an info issue.

docs.title: 3. Business priors and lift tests
docs.text:
Users state what they already believe in business units (BusinessPriors):

calibration:
  business_priors:
    channels:
      tv:     {roi: [1.5, 4.0], credibility: 0.8}   # every euro returns 1.5-4 euros, 80% sure
      search: {roi: [2.0, 6.0], credibility: 0.9}
      social: {contribution_share: [0.02, 0.10]}    # 2-10% of revenue
    baseline_share: {share: [0.5, 0.8]}
  lift_tests:
    - {id: tv-holdout-2026q2, channel: tv, geo: de, start: 2026-04-06, end: 2026-05-03,
       spend_delta: -120000, kpi_delta: -260000, ci: [-380000, -140000], ci_level: 0.9}
  • Credibility is the probability that the truth lies inside the range. A range [low, high] at credibility c becomes a log-normal (ROI) or logit-normal (share) whose central c interval is exactly that range (lognormal_from_range).
  • Shares must fit inside the KPI: the smallest shares (channels plus baseline) cannot add up to more than 100% (BUSINESS_PRIORS_INVALID).
  • At least one belief is stated, but any one will do: baseline_share alone (no channels) narrows only the baseline, and channels without a belief keep the model's default priors.
  • Lift tests are experiment results used as calibration data: extra (or removed) spend on one channel, optionally in one geo, over a window, and the incremental KPI it caused with a standard error or confidence interval. The model treats each as an extra observation of the channel's incremental effect.
  • Only models that declare them (Capabilities.calibration) accept them; otherwise static validation reports CALIBRATION_UNSUPPORTED.

Turning beliefs into model-space priors needs the data's scale and the model's transforms, so it runs in the sandbox as a translate_priors run (POST /v1/guided/prior-translations). Its result (PriorTranslationResult) holds the priors to write at /model/settings/priors (apply_prior_translation) and a prior-predictive preview in business units: ROI and contribution-share distributions per channel, the baseline share and a KPI fan - so users see what their beliefs imply before fitting. The math, the lift-test likelihood and the checks each layer runs are in Guided modelling.

docs.title: 4. Run, then the sanity scorecard
docs.text: Every fit gets a Scorecard of plain-language checks, each pass, warn or fail, with the measured value, the threshold, a message_plain, a suggested action and a link back to this page. overall is the worst item. Templates choose their checks and may tighten thresholds. The catalog is mapi_spec.scorecard.SCORECARD_CHECKS:

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text: Check Metric Thresholds What to do convergence.rhat (Chains agree) r_hat_max warn above 1.01, fail above 1.05 Run more tuning and draws, or simplify the model. convergence.ess (Enough independent draws) ess_bulk_min warn below 400, fail below 100 Increase the number of draws. convergence.divergences (Sampler stayed on track) divergence_rate warn above 0%, fail above 1% Raise target_accept, or use more informative priors.

docs.title: Holdout error
docs.text:
Check Metric Thresholds What to do holdout.mape (Holdout error) mape warn above 10%, fail above 25% Check the last periods of data for gaps or one-off events, and add holidays or controls that explain them. holdout.coverage_90 (Uncertainty is honest) coverage_90 warn when more than 10% away from 90%, fail when more than 25% away Look for trends or shifts the model does not capture. holdout.hit_rate (Beats a naive guess) accuracy_lift warn below +2 points, fail below -10 points Add what drives the choice for every product (price, promotions, displays), or collect more trips per customer.

holdout.hit_rate is the check of the customer_choice template: on each household's held-out trip, the model's most likely product is compared with the product bought (accuracy, the hit rate) and with always guessing the most popular product of the held-out trips (accuracy_naive - a strict baseline, since it knows the holdout's own shares). accuracy_lift is the difference in percentage points. The template also reports the log_score (mean log probability of the bought product; higher is better) and the multi-class brier score (0 is perfect) in the model's metrics.

docs.title: Plausibility
docs.text: Check Metric Thresholds What to do plausibility.negative_roi (No channel loses money) negative_roi_share warn above 10%, fail above 50% Check the channel's spend data, or state an ROI range in business priors. plausibility.roi_absurd (Returns are believable) roi_max warn above 20, fail above 100 Check spend units and gaps, or state an ROI range in business priors. plausibility.share_outlier (No channel dominates) max_channel_share warn above 60%, fail above 90% Check for a missing control (price, promotions, seasonality). plausibility.baseline_share (Baseline is plausible) baseline_share warn when more than 40% away from 50%, fail when more than 48% away State a baseline share in business priors, or review the controls. plausibility.prior_overlap (The data informed the model) prior_overlap_max warn above 90%, fail above 99% Add data that varies the driver (or a lift test), or state a business prior you trust for it.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Check Metric Thresholds What to do data.missing (Few missing values) missing_fraction warn above 5%, fail above 30% Fill the gaps in the source data, or drop the affected series. data.history (Enough history) history_years warn below 2 years, fail below 1 year (the weekly_forecast template: below 0.5) Add more history if you have it. data.spend_variation (Spend varies enough) spend_cv_min warn below 10%, fail below 2% Add a lift test for the channel, or state its ROI in business priors.

How the runner measures each check is in Guided modelling. The scorecard also gates promotion to an endpoint: see Integrations.

docs.title: 5. What-if sliders
docs.text:
Sliders answer instantly because every MMM fit precomputes per-draw response grids (ResponseGridView, ui/grids/response_curves.json, format mapi.response-grid/v1): for each thinned posterior draw, channel and spend multiplier, the channel's total contribution over the fit window, the spend at each grid point, the actual spend and the baseline.

A WhatIfScenario sets a multiplier per channel (1 = what was actually spent). The interpolation contract, shared by the web app and mapi_spec.whatif.evaluate_scenario:

  1. a channel without a multiplier keeps 1; multipliers outside the grid are refused (SCENARIO_OUT_OF_RANGE) - the grid is never extrapolated;
  2. per draw and channel, the contribution is interpolated linearly between the two grid points around the multiplier, and so is spend;
  3. per draw, KPI = baseline + the channels' contributions, and the change is taken against all multipliers at 1; means and quantiles are computed after summing, so the uncertainty band stays joint across channels.

The web app answers the sliders in the browser with a TypeScript port of this contract, which its unit tests check against golden cases the spec tests export (packages/spec/tests/snapshots/whatif_golden.json).

Run exact turns the scenario into a counterfactual score request with one multiply intervention per changed channel and submits a real score run (POST /v1/guided/requests:compile, then score).

docs.title: Forecasts and counterfactuals
docs.text: Guided forecasts (forecast_request) ask for a horizon and a policy for covariates whose future the user did not supply (ScoreRequest.future_covariates): carry_last (default in Guided mode), seasonal_naive, zero, or supplied with a scenario dataset. Intervention presets build counterfactuals in one click: channel off (ChannelOff: that channel's spend set to zero) and budget × k (BudgetScale: every, or the listed, channel's spend scaled by k), over the fit window or over a forecast horizon. Responses default to expected values with the mean and a 90% interval (Q2).

docs.title: Integrations v0.4
docs.text: A fitted model is only useful once other applications can use it: a planning tool scores budgets, a spreadsheet pulls a forecast, a dashboard embeds a chart, a pipeline hears when a fit finishes. This page explains the integration concepts of v0.4 and the contracts in mapi_spec behind them; the endpoints are in the HTTP API reference, and Endpoints and webhooks walks through them with curl.

docs.title: Endpoints and aliases
docs.text:
An endpoint is a stable alias for one model version: endpoint://growth/geo-mmm-prod. Integrations call the alias, so a better model can be promoted - or a bad one rolled back - without touching them. Every promotion and rollback is a numbered revision in the endpoint's history, with who did it and why.
