PUT /v1/endpoints/geo-mmm-prod
X-Mapi-Project: acme/growth

{"model": "model://growth/eu-geo-mmm@v3", "expected_revision": 3}

docs.title: The promotion gate
docs.text:
Promotion is gated on the sanity scorecard and the endpoint's EvaluationPolicy (mapi_spec.scorecard.promotion_gate):

The version Gate What happens Scorecard passes allowed Promoted Scorecard warns, or has no scorecard; an evaluate_then_refit fit whose scorecard measured no holdout check (no data.split, or no evaluate.metrics: it was never evaluated); a guided version whose template's checks did not all run (NOT_EVALUATED) needs_override 409 OVERRIDE_REQUIRED unless a signed-in project admin sends override: true with a reason; the override is audited (endpoint.promote_override) Scorecard fails, the fit was interrupted (partial) blocked 409 PROMOTION_BLOCKED; no override Fitted train_only blocked Endpoints need evaluate_then_refit (Q13): context and terminal state come from all the data. A policy with fit_mode: train_only accepts exploration fits Expects input the callers do not send blocked (policy schema_change: block), needs_override (warn) or ignored (allow) A dim removed or changed, a tightened dim policy, a new required input, an input whose dims or type changed (schema_breaks)

Overriding is a human decision: the manage permission on endpoints belongs to project admins and no token scope grants it, not even admin. An endpoints:promote token (for CI) can promote passing versions and roll back, never override.

docs.title: Scoring an endpoint
docs.text:
POST /v1/endpoints/{alias}/score takes an EndpointScoreCall: a score request without model. data and scenario may be dataset:// references or small inline XrJSON datasets (xr.Dataset.to_dict() shape, up to 5 MB), so spreadsheets and scripts need no upload. The control plane only checks the envelope of inline data (names, nesting, sizes); the values are decoded in the sandbox. Send Prefer: wait=60 to get the result in the response when the run finishes in time (200), otherwise 202 with the run to follow. GET …/schema describes what to send (EndpointSchema: the input schema frozen at promotion, score modes, dims and an example payload) and POST …/validate checks a call without running it.

A score:<alias> token can read the endpoint, its schema and snippets, and score it - and nothing else.

docs.title: Snippets
docs.text:
GET /v1/endpoints/{alias}/snippets returns ready-to-run code that scores the endpoint with its example payload, in Python (mapi-client), TypeScript (fetch), curl, R (httr2), Google Sheets (Apps Script), Atlas (RemoteModel) and a notebook cell (Client().endpoint(alias).score(...), which returns an xarray.Dataset). The generators are pure functions (mapi_spec.snippets.render_snippets), so the server, the CLI, the web app and these docs produce the same code: the Integrations hub shows and copies the server's snippets verbatim. Snippets never contain a secret: they read the token from MAPI_TOKEN (a script property in Apps Script). Every value is embedded with the language's own literal syntax, and tests parse the generated code back to prove a hostile payload cannot escape its string.

curl -sS -X POST 'https://api.mapi.example/v1/endpoints/geo-mmm-prod/score' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAPI_TOKEN" \
  -H 'X-Mapi-Project: acme/growth' \
  -H 'Prefer: wait=60' \
  --data '{"mode": "forecast", "horizon": {"dim": "time", "periods": 8},
           "future_covariates": "carry_last"}'

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
A webhook calls your URL when something happens in a project:

Event When run.succeeded, run.failed A run finished model.version.ready A fit produced a model version (with its scorecard verdict) endpoint.promoted An alias points at a new version (promotion or rollback) score.completed A score run finished tenant.deletion.completed The tenant was purged (the last event it sends)

Each delivery is a JSON envelope {id, type, created, tenant, project, api_version, data}. Envelopes carry ids and states, never data values, signed URLs or secrets - fetch results with the API.

docs.title: Verifying a delivery
docs.text:
Deliveries are signed with the webhook's secret (shown once, when the webhook is created or its secret rotated):

Mapi-Signature: t=1792000000,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd

v1 is the hex HMAC-SHA256 of "<t>.<raw body>". Recompute it over the raw body, compare in constant time, and refuse timestamps more than 300 seconds from your clock - that bounds replays. During a rotation the header carries one v1 per active secret.

from mapi_spec.webhooks import verify_signature

if not verify_signature(raw_body, request.headers["Mapi-Signature"], secret):
    return 401

Failed deliveries are retried after 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h. A receiver that answers 410 Gone is disabled at once, and a webhook is disabled after 20 consecutive failed events. The delivery log shows every attempt (status, response code, duration) and any delivery can be replayed.

docs.title: SSRF protection
docs.text:
A webhook URL is a request the platform makes on a tenant's behalf, so the server only delivers under a strict policy (mapi_spec.webhooks.SSRF_POLICY):

  • https only, on port 443 or 8443, with no credentials or fragment in the URL, and a host name - never an IP literal, localhost or an internal suffix (.internal, .local, ...);
  • the server resolves the host itself and refuses if any address is private, loopback, link-local, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), CGNAT, unique-local, multicast or otherwise not globally routable - including IPv4 addresses embedded in IPv6;
  • it then connects to the address it checked (no second lookup, so DNS rebinding cannot swap it), follows no redirects, gives up after 5 seconds and reads at most 256 KiB of the answer.

A URL that breaks the policy is refused with 422 WEBHOOK_URL_BLOCKED; one that starts resolving to a blocked address later fails its deliveries as blocked and is audited as a security signal (webhook.url_blocked).

docs.title: Plots: rendering, sharing and embeds
docs.text:
• Saved plots keep a model version's plot, or a plot you wrote, under a name.
  • Static rendering (POST /v1/plots:render) produces PNG, SVG or PDF in the sandbox for reports: vl-convert for Vega-Lite, with network access off; Plotly needs kaleido and a Chrome in the runner image and is refused with MODE_NOT_SUPPORTED until an operator enables it.
  • Embed links are tokenised, read-only and expiring, for BI tools, Slack and Notion. The token is shown once, links can be revoked, and allowed_origins limits which sites may frame them. Only platform recipes can be embedded - plots the platform's own recipes rendered from a model version - never plots written by a plugin or a user: a sandboxed iframe can still navigate itself, so shared views only ever run code the platform wrote. Requests for anything else get 422 EMBED_NOT_ALLOWED; expired or revoked links answer 410 LINK_EXPIRED. The link opens the plot sandbox's embed page, which may fetch nothing but the API's public embed view. See Sharing plots.

docs.title: The trust lifecycle
docs.text:
Public sign-up opens with cut line A: public tenants run declarative specs and built-in plugins only - untrusted data, trusted code.

  1. Sign-up takes an e-mail, a name and accepted terms. The answer is the same for new and known addresses, so it cannot be used to find accounts; disposable e-mail domains are refused through a pluggable policy hook.
  2. E-mail verification with a single-use link (valid 24 hours) creates a public-tier tenant with a default project, the new user as its admin.
  3. Identity verification is required before any uploaded code: tenants on the verified tier (allow-listed, M4) once verified, public tenants only after cut line B (M5). Until then VerificationStatus.uploaded_code_allowed is false for every public tenant.
  4. Deleting a tenant is scheduled with a 7-day grace period in which the tenant is suspended (read-only) and the deletion can be cancelled. Then every store is purged - database rows, objects, queued work, logs and webhooks - with progress shown per store. The audit log (pseudonymised) and the cost ledger (amounts only, for tax law) are kept for their legal retention.
  5. A GDPR export packages everything the tenant stored into one archive with a short-lived download link. A suspended tenant can still ask for it.

docs.title: Labelled data
docs.text:
Every model on modeling-api reads one xr.Dataset: variables with named dims, and dims with coordinate labels. Nothing is positional, so the platform can reorder, subset, extend and add labels safely, and you can score data whose stores are in a different order than at fit time.

A DataSchema describes such a dataset: what each dim is and what may happen to it at score time, and what each variable means to a model.

docs.title: A schema in one look
docs.text:
layout: dense                       # or: long (one row per observation + *_idx variables)
dims:
  market:  {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
  channel: {kind: categorical, policy: fixed}
  date:    {kind: time, policy: extend, freq: D}
vars:
  revenue: {dims: [market, date], dtype: float64, role: target, units: EUR}
  spend:   {dims: [market, channel, date], dtype: float64, role: spend, units: EUR,
            future_required: true}

docs.title: Dims and their policies
docs.text:
The policy is the heart of the contract: it says what a score request may do with a dim.

Policy For At score time Typical errors fixed channels, products, states Only labels seen at fit (any subset, any order) UNSEEN_LEVELS extend time, observation index New labels appended after the fitted range, without gaps, up to max_extension NON_CONTIGUOUS_EXTENSION, COORD_NOT_ALLOWED, HORIZON_EXCEEDS_FIT new_levels markets, stores, counties, households Unseen labels allowed, handled by new_level_strategy UNSEEN_LEVELS when the strategy is error

new_level_strategy decides what an unseen level becomes:

Strategy Meaning Example hyperprior A fresh draw from the fitted population distribution, per posterior draw A new market in a hierarchical MMM: honest, wider uncertainty pooled The population average (or a frequency-weighted average of fitted levels) A new store in an xgboost demand model zero The level contributes nothing A new category in a one-hot model error Rejected The default

Other DimSpec fields:

  • kind: categorical, time, integer, float or index;
  • freq: a pandas frequency for time dims (D, W-SUN, MS), so the platform can generate forecast coordinates and check contiguity;
  • max_extension: how many periods a forecast may reach past the fit without a refit;
  • ordered: whether a categorical dim has a meaningful order.

Policies only tighten

A model's schema template declares the loosest policy it can handle; your data's schema and the spec's dim_policies may only make it tighter (fixed is the tightest). Trying to loosen it is DIM_POLICY_LOOSENED.

docs.title: Variables and roles
docs.text:
Field Meaning dims, dtype The shape contract (float64, int64, bool, str, datetime64[ns], …) role What the variable means: target, covariate, media, spend, control, index, mask, constant, weight, exposure units A pint-style string (EUR, units, 1). Steps update it (fx_convert → EUR, scaling → 1), and outputs report it missing forbid (default), allow (NaN is fine) or mask (a mask variable marks valid cells) missing_sentinel A code such as -99.99 that means "missing" and is turned into NaN by core.replace_sentinel future_required Must be supplied over a forecast horizon (planned prices, promotions, budgets) index_of Long layout: this integer variable indexes that dim (county_idx(obs) → county) bounds Allowed value range, checked in plain language

Roles let plugins and plot templates work across datasets: "every spend variable", "the target over time, one line per geo".

docs.title: Two layouts for ragged data
docs.text:
Real panels are often ragged: households have different numbers of trips, animals different track lengths. A schema uses one of two canonical forms, and the built-in steps core.to_long and core.to_padded convert between them.

LongPadded

One row per observation along an obs dim, plus index variables:

layout: long
dims:
  obs:    {kind: integer, policy: extend}
  county: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: hyperprior}
vars:
  log_radon:  {dims: [obs], dtype: float64, role: target}
  county_idx: {dims: [obs], dtype: int64, role: index, index_of: county}

A dense cube plus a mask variable:

dims:
  animal: {kind: categorical, policy: new_levels, new_level_strategy: pooled}
  step:   {kind: integer, policy: extend}
vars:
  y:    {dims: [animal, step], dtype: float64, role: target, missing: mask}
  mask: {dims: [animal, step], dtype: bool, role: mask}
ragged:
  - {group_dim: animal, within_dim: step, form: padded, mask_var: mask}

docs.title: Draft a schema from data
docs.text:
infer_schema gives you a starting point: time dims become extend with an inferred frequency, other dims fixed, variables covariate unless you say otherwise.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from mapi_sdk import infer_schema, validate_dataset
from mapi_spec import DimPolicy

days = pd.date_range("2026-03-01", periods=28, freq="D")
markets = ["DE", "FR", "UK"]
channels = ["tv", "search"]
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
media = xr.Dataset(
    {
        "revenue": (("market", "date"), rng.gamma(50.0, 20.0, (3, 28))),
        "spend": (("market", "channel", "date"), rng.gamma(5.0, 100.0, (3, 2, 28))),
    },
    coords={"market": markets, "channel": channels, "date": days},
)

schema = infer_schema(
    media,
    targets=["revenue"],
    policies={"market": "new_levels"},
    units={"revenue": "EUR", "spend": "EUR"},
)
print(schema.dims["date"].policy, schema.dims["date"].freq)  # extend D
print(schema.dims["channel"].policy)  # fixed
print(schema.vars["revenue"].role)  # target

docs.title: Data checks in plain language
docs.text:
validate_dataset checks a dataset against its schema and describes every problem for a non-expert reader. Fitting and scoring run the same checks and stop on errors.

broken = media.copy(deep=True)
broken["revenue"].loc[{"market": ["FR", "UK"], "date": days[10:12]}] = np.nan

for issue in validate_dataset(schema, broken):
    print(issue.severity, issue.code, "-", issue.message)
# error SCHEMA_INVALID - 2 markets are missing 2 days of revenue in March 2026

docs.title: Binding: your names, the model's names
docs.text:
Steps and models are written against canonical names (geo, time, y, spend). A spec's data.bind maps them to your dataset's names. The binding is stored in the bundle and reversed on every output, so results come back in your vocabulary.

from mapi_sdk import BindingMap

binding = BindingMap({"dims": {"geo": "market", "time": "date"}, "vars": {"y": "revenue"}})
canonical = binding.apply(media)  # what steps and models see
print(sorted(canonical.dims))  # ['channel', 'geo', 'time']
print(sorted(binding.reverse(canonical).dims))  # ['channel', 'date', 'market'] - your names

data:
  bind:
    dims: {geo: market, time: date}     # canonical: yours
    vars: {y: revenue, spend: spend}

docs.title: Side tables
docs.text:
Small constant datasets that steps read (FX rates, holiday calendars) are side tables, declared in the spec with a score-time policy:

score_policy At score time pinned The exact version used at fit time (holidays) latest The latest version of the table supplied The score request must name the table (request.side_tables), e.g. FX rates for the forecast period

A step that needs a table with too little coverage fails with SIDE_TABLE_COVERAGE.

docs.title: Wire formats
docs.text:
Format Use API XrJSON Small payloads, curl, TypeScript: the Dataset.to_dict() shape with explicit dtypes and caps mapi_sdk.wire.to_xrjson / from_xrjson zarr zip Datasets and trees as single objects (zarr v3, deterministic bytes, zstd/blosc only) write_zarr_zip, read_zarr_zip, write_datatree_zip, read_datatree_zip Arrow IPC Tidy tables for UI views and plots mapi_sdk.wire.to_arrow_table pickle Never, across any boundary –

Next: Pipelines and stages.

docs.title: Pipelines, stages and replay
docs.text:
A pipeline is an ordered list of steps. Each step is a small, versioned transform with typed settings and, if it learns something, a fitted state. The promise of the platform is simple to state and fiddly to keep:

Scoring replays exactly the preprocessing that was learned at fit time. It never refits.

This page explains the pieces that keep that promise: stages, the split stage, context tails, inverse transforms and scenario entry points.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
A step implements fit (learn, on train only), transform (apply; never learns) and, when it can, inverse. A complete one, from the porting guide:

A scaling step, in full 
from typing import ClassVar

from mapi_sdk import Step, StepContext, StepSettings, StepState
from mapi_spec import StepKind
from pydantic import Field, JsonValue


class ScaleSettings(StepSettings):
    vars: list[str]
    over: list[str] = Field(default=[])  # plain defaults: the exported JSON Schema keeps them
    unseen_levels: str = "error"  # error | pooled | fill: what a new level's scale becomes
    fill_value: float = 1.0  # the scale used by 'fill'


class ScaleStep(Step[ScaleSettings, StepState]):
    """Divide each variable by its mean absolute value over `over` (learned on train)."""

    id = "acme.scale"
    version = "1.0.0"
    kind = StepKind.VALUE
    Settings = ScaleSettings
    State = StepState  # stateful: fitted on the training data only
    invertible = True
    var_params = ("vars",)  # settings that name variables ...
    dim_params = ("over",)  # ... and dims, so the control plane can check them
    unseen_levels_param = "unseen_levels"
    effect_template: ClassVar[dict[str, JsonValue]] = {  # static: how the schema changes
        "template_params": ["vars"],
        "updates": {"{*vars as v}": {"units": "1"}},
    }
    summary = "Divide by the mean absolute value over the named dims"  # catalog and UI text
    summary_plain = "Puts each series on a comparable scale"

    def fit(self, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, ctx: StepContext) -> StepState:
        return StepState(arrays=xr.Dataset({f"scale__{v}": abs(ds[v]).mean(s.over) for v in s.vars}))

    def _scale(self, v: str, ds: xr.Dataset, s: ScaleSettings, st: StepState, ctx: StepContext):
        state = st.array(f"scale__{v}")
        return ctx.align_state(state, ds, s.unseen_levels, fill_value=s.fill_value)

    def transform(self, ds, s, st, ctx):  # never learns; skips absent vars (the target at score)
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] / self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

    def inverse(self, ds, s, st, ctx):
        return ds.assign({v: ds[v] * self._scale(v, ds, s, st, ctx) for v in s.vars if v in ds})

Every step has a kind:

Kind Changes Inverted on the way out? Examples reshape Structure: dims, frequency, layout Never resample, to_long, stack, filter_coords value Values of existing variables Yes, if invertible fx_convert, mean_scale, standardize, log1p feature Adds new variables Not needed lag, fourier, calendar, one_hot, formula

And a static schema effect: a JSON template that says how the step changes the schema (adds lag dim, sets units to 1, turns daily date into weekly time). The control plane uses it to propagate the schema through the whole pipeline without running anything.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
A stage is the dataset after a named step; raw is the bound input. Static validation computes the schema at every stage, so problems surface before any data is read:

from mapi_plugin_mmm.examples import E33_SPEC_YAML, e33_dataset, e33_raw_schema
from mapi_sdk import default_registry
from mapi_spec import load_model_spec, validate_spec

catalog = default_registry().catalog()  # static JSON: settings schemas + schema effects
data, _ = e33_dataset(weeks=12)
raw_schema = e33_raw_schema(data)

check = validate_spec(load_model_spec(E33_SPEC_YAML), catalog, raw_schema)
rs = check.resolved
for stage, schema in rs.stages.items():
    y, time = schema.vars["y"], schema.dims["time"]
    print(f"{stage:12} time={time.freq:6} y in {y.units:4} dims={', '.join(schema.dims)}")
# raw          time=D      y in LCU  dims=geo, channel, time
# to_eur       time=D      y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# weekly       time=W-SUN  y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# scale_spend  time=W-SUN  y in EUR  dims=geo, channel, time
# scale_y      time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time
# lags         time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag
# season       time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag, fourier_mode
# hols         time=W-SUN  y in 1    dims=geo, channel, time, lag, fourier_mode
print(rs.split_stage)  # weekly: the holdout is cut in whole weeks
print(rs.last_reshape_stage)  # weekly: outputs are inverted back to weekly EUR, not days

Stages are how specs refer to points in the pipeline:

  • data.split.after_step: where the train/holdout split happens;
  • ScoreRequest.inputs_stage: where a scenario enters the pipeline;
  • the output space: the stage outputs are inverted back to.

docs.title: Where the split happens
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["raw<br/>daily, LCU"] --> FX["to_eur<br/><i>stateless</i>"]
    FX --> W["weekly<br/><i>stateless reshape</i>"]
    W --> SPLIT{{"split<br/>last 8 weeks"}}
    SPLIT -->|train| SC["scale_spend, scale_y<br/><i>learn on train</i>"]
    SPLIT -.->|holdout| SC
    SC --> L["lags<br/><i>context tail</i>"]
    L --> M["model"]
    style SPLIT fill:#5eead4,stroke:#0f766e,color:#1e1b4b

Some dims only exist after preprocessing: a holdout of "the last 8 weeks" cannot be cut from daily data before it is resampled. So the split happens at a stage. If after_step is not given, it defaults to the end of the stateless prefix, the leading steps that learn nothing (unit conversion, resampling).

If a step that learns runs before the split, its state would be learned partly from the holdout and the evaluation would be optimistic. Validation reports it:

leaky = E33_SPEC_YAML.replace("after_step: weekly", "after_step: scale_y")
for issue in validate_spec(load_model_spec(leaky), catalog, raw_schema).errors:
    print(issue.code, issue.pointer)
    print("  ", issue.message)
# LEAKAGE_RISK /data/split/after_step
#    stateful step 'scale_spend' (pipeline[2]) runs before the split at stage 'scale_y';
#    its state would be learned from holdout data
# LEAKAGE_RISK /data/split/after_step
#    stateful step 'scale_y' (pipeline[3]) runs before the split at stage 'scale_y'; ...

Set allow_leakage: true on the split to downgrade the error to an acknowledged warning.

docs.title: Evaluate the way you will forecast
docs.text:
fit.mode: evaluate_then_refit (the default) does this:

sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Data
    participant P as Pipeline + model
    participant B as Bundles
    D->>P: stateless prefix on all data, then split at the split stage
    P->>P: fit step states + model on TRAIN
    P->>P: score HOLDOUT through the score path<br/>(context tails from train)
    P->>B: evaluation bundle + metrics
    P->>P: refit states + model on ALL data
    P->>B: production bundle (links evaluation + metrics)

The holdout is never scored by a separate code path: it goes through score_bundle, with the context it would have in production. Then everything is refitted on all data, so the context tails and terminal states that forecasts start from are the latest ones. train_only stops after evaluation and keeps the train fit.

docs.title: Context tails: looking back across the fit boundary
docs.text:
Steps that look back in time (lags, carry-over) declare a context need, for example {along: time, n: 6, within: [geo]}. At fit time the step stores the last n rows of its own input stage, per group. At score time the platform prepends them before transforming, checks that the new data continues the fitted range, and drops them from the output.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Fit
        T1["… w49 w50 w51 w52"] --> TAIL["stored tail per geo:<br/>w47–w52 (weekly, scaled)"]
    end
    subgraph Score
        TAIL --> CAT["w47–w52 ‖ w53 w54 w55 w56"]
        NEW["forecast payload<br/>w53–w56"] --> CAT
        CAT --> LAG["lag_tensor"] --> DROP["drop context rows"] --> OUT["w53–w56 with<br/>real carry-over"]
    end

The result is identical to transforming the whole series at once; the contract kit checks this "context-window equivalence" for every step and model. A new market has no tail, so its lags are padded according to the step's settings (pad: first).

Sequential models (HMMs, Kalman filters) keep a model-side terminal state instead; see Forecasting.

docs.title: Inverse transforms and the output space
docs.text:
On the way out, the platform undoes invertible value steps in reverse order and stops at the last reshape step. A model fitted on weekly, scaled EUR returns weekly EUR: scaling can be undone, the weekly resample cannot (daily values are not recoverable from weekly sums).

Every output records where it ended up:

Attribute Example Meaning output_space {"y_hat": "weekly"} The stage the values live at units EUR Units after inversion retransform {"y_hat": "median"} For point models through a non-linear inverse: the inverse of a mean is not a mean, so the value is labelled (or Duan smearing is used)

Ask for output: {units: model} to skip inversion, for example to get contributions that add up exactly through a log1p.

docs.title: Scenarios enter at a stage
docs.text:
A planner should not have to invent daily local-currency spend to ask about a weekly EUR budget. ScoreRequest.inputs_stage lets data enter the pipeline after a named step; the steps before it, and the side tables they need, are skipped:

mode: forecast
horizon: {dim: time, periods: 8}
inputs_stage: weekly        # send weekly EUR spend; to_eur and the FX table are skipped

The E33 conformance fixture checks that this gives exactly the same forecast as the raw daily path for the same spend.

docs.title: Models that own their preprocessing
docs.text: Some models do their own scaling or carry-over (pymc-marketing's MMM does both). They declare owns: [scaling, carryover, inverse_units] in their capabilities, the platform steps aside, and outputs are labelled as already in original units. See the pymc-marketing adapter.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
A lag of the target is a recursive feature: forecasting more periods than the smallest lag would need predictions as inputs. v1 forecasts are direct, so such specs are rejected with RECURSIVE_UNSUPPORTED unless the model declares owns: [recursion].

Next: Representations and summaries.

docs.title: Quotas and cost v0.3
docs.text: A public modelling platform's real cost risk is compute: an accidental 500-task sweep, a leaked token, or someone mining on free fits. From v0.3 every run is estimated before it starts, checked against quotas at three levels, scheduled fairly against everyone else's work, and metered into a cost ledger when it ends. The contracts are in mapi_spec.quotas, mapi_spec.cost and mapi_spec.admin.

docs.title: Quotas are vCPU-seconds
docs.text:
Compute is limited in vCPU-seconds, not runs: a two-minute fit on class S (2 vCPU) uses 240 vCPU-seconds, a five-minute fit on class M (4 vCPU) 1,200. Each limit below is optional; an unset limit means "no limit at this level".

Limit Kind Notes vcpu_seconds_per_day, vcpu_seconds_per_month Cumulative, UTC day and month Checked against the run's estimate at submit concurrent_runs Live count Runs between queued and a terminal state max_fanout_tasks Per submission Caps one sweep, backtest or SBC (taskCount) max_resource_class Per submission For example, the free tier runs on class S only storage_bytes Cumulative Dataset versions, uploads in progress and model bundles (every model version's stored objects) egress_bytes_per_month Cumulative, UTC month Downloads: the size of every object the API hands out a signed link to (dataset and model artifacts, ui/ views, score and render outputs), and of public embed views. Charged when the link is minted; GDPR exports are never charged requests_per_minute Rate API calls

docs.title: Three levels
docs.text:
Every request is checked against up to three policies, most specific first:

  1. Token: the token's own rate limit and vCPU-second budget (set when it was minted).
  2. Tenant: the tenant's policy, or the defaults of its trust tier.
  3. Global: platform-wide limits that protect the cloud project itself (Cloud Run allows 1,000 running executions per region; the global default stops at 700).

The first limit a request would exceed decides the answer:

Code HTTP When What the client does RATE_LIMITED 429 Too many requests per minute at any level Wait Retry-After seconds and retry QUOTA_EXCEEDED 429 Any other limit Read detail (which level, which limit); Retry-After is set when the limit resets with the UTC day or month

Cumulative limits only block requests that ask for more: a tenant over its storage quota can still read, download and delete.

from datetime import UTC, datetime

from mapi_spec.quotas import (
    QuotaDemand,
    QuotaLimits,
    QuotaPolicy,
    QuotaScope,
    QuotaUsage,
    evaluate_quota,
)
from mapi_spec.resources import ResourceClass

now = datetime(2026, 10, 15, 22, 0, tzinfo=UTC)
tenant = QuotaPolicy(
    scope=QuotaScope.TENANT,
    subject_id="acme",
    limits=QuotaLimits(vcpu_seconds_per_day=86_400, max_resource_class=ResourceClass.L),
)
used = QuotaUsage(vcpu_seconds_today=85_000)

fit = QuotaDemand(new_runs=1, vcpu_seconds=2_400, resource_class=ResourceClass.M)
decision = evaluate_quota([(tenant, used)], fit, now=now)
print(decision.allowed, decision.code, decision.limit_name)
# False QUOTA_EXCEEDED vcpu_seconds_per_day
print(decision.retry_after_seconds)  # 7200: the UTC day resets in two hours
print(decision.to_problem().status, decision.headers())  # 429 {'Retry-After': '7200'}

Default tenant limits by trust tier (operators override them per tenant with PUT /v1/admin/quotas):

Tier vCPU-s / day vCPU-s / month Concurrent runs Fan-out tasks Largest class Requests / min public 3,600 36,000 2 16 S 60 verified 86,400 1,000,000 20 256 L 600 internal — — 100 1,000 — 6,000 self-hosted-trusted — — — — — —

Returned draws. A score request returns a summary by default (no draws). Draws on request (output.draws) are capped per tier: at most 300 on public, 500 on every other tier (mapi_spec.quotas.MAX_SCORE_DRAWS). More is refused with QUOTA_EXCEEDED at /output/draws, whether the call comes through POST /v1/models/…:score, an endpoint, or its …/validate; the score job carries the cap and the runner enforces it again.

docs.title: Interactive and batch work
docs.text:
Each run has a priority class:

  • interactive: score, render, derive, validate and describe runs. Someone is usually waiting for them.
  • batch: fits, ingest, evaluation, optimisation and fan-out parents.

The dispatcher leases queued runs with weighted fair sharing. For each candidate it computes (tenant's running tasks + the run's tasks) / (tenant weight × class weight), with weight 4 for interactive and 1 for batch, and leases the smallest first, until the free capacity (and the Cloud Run jobs.run rate, 180 calls a minute) is used up. A tenant with 40 tasks running has to wait behind an idle tenant's score, and a 200-task SBC fills in the capacity left over instead of blocking everyone:

from datetime import timedelta

from mapi_spec.quotas import LeaseCandidate, PriorityClass, plan_leases

t0 = datetime(2026, 10, 15, tzinfo=UTC)
queue = [
    LeaseCandidate(f"sbc_{i}", "acme", PriorityClass.BATCH, t0 + timedelta(seconds=i))
    for i in range(200)
] + [LeaseCandidate("score_1", "beta", PriorityClass.INTERACTIVE, t0 + timedelta(minutes=5))]

picked = plan_leases(queue, capacity=3, running_tasks={"acme": 40})
print([c.run_id for c in picked])  # ['score_1', 'sbc_0', 'sbc_1']

When the backend itself answers 429, the dispatcher backs off exponentially (1, 2, 4 … 64 seconds, never less than a Retry-After) and submits exactly once when the limit clears.

docs.title: Prices and the cost ledger
docs.text:
Every run's cost is computed from its resource class and wall time:

  • vCPU-seconds = vCPUs of the class × billed seconds × tasks;
  • GiB-seconds = memory of the class × billed seconds × tasks;
  • billed seconds = wall time rounded up to 100 ms.

Prices come from a versioned price table. The default mirrors Cloud Run's list prices, 0.000018 USD per vCPU-second and 0.000002 USD per GiB-second; a deployment sets its own. Unit prices are integer nanos and amounts are integer micros (1 USD = 1,000,000 micros), so every amount is exact and can be recomputed from its ledger row. Every amount names the price-table version used: new prices never rewrite old costs.

from mapi_spec.cost import DEFAULT_PRICE_TABLE, estimate_cost, format_micros

est = estimate_cost(ResourceClass.M, wall_seconds=300)  # an E33-style fit, five minutes on M
print(est.vcpu_seconds, est.gib_seconds)  # 1200.0 4800.0
print(est.amount_micros, format_micros(est.amount_micros, est.currency))  # 31200 0.031200 USD
print(est.price_version == DEFAULT_PRICE_TABLE.version)  # True

sweep = estimate_cost(ResourceClass.S, wall_seconds=120, task_count=50)
print(format_micros(sweep.amount_micros, sweep.currency))  # 0.312000 USD

The cost ledger is append-only. Each finished attempt adds one actual entry with its run, attempt, resource class, task count, wall time, vCPU- and GiB-seconds, price version and amount. Operators can add adjustment entries (for example, a refund after an infrastructure failure). A run's cost field folds its entries together:

Run.cost field Meaning estimated true until the first attempt has been metered estimate_micros The estimate made at submit amount_micros, currency The total so far, over all attempts vcpu_seconds, gib_seconds The metered usage price_version The price table used attempts_billed How many attempts have been metered usd Kept from v0.2: the amount in dollars when the currency is USD

GET /v1/usage reports a project's ledger totals for a UTC day or month (grouped by resource class, day, token or run) and where it stands against each quota. Tenant admins see the whole tenant at GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/usage. Operators see cost by tenant for the whole platform at GET /v1/admin/usage (the Cost tab of the admin console).

Retries are capped by cost as well as by count: an infrastructure failure is retried automatically only while what the run has cost (its metered attempts plus the attempt that just failed) stays below MAPI_AUTO_RETRY_COST_FACTOR (default 2) times its estimate, at most MAPI_MAX_INFRA_RETRIES times. A retry resumes from the newest checkpoints any earlier attempt wrote, and a run that has already used more than 30 minutes is only retried with the user's consent.

docs.title: Kill switches
docs.text:
Operators have two platform-wide switches (PUT /v1/admin/kill-switches, audited, a reason is required):

Switch Effect untrusted_execution_enabled When off, no run of tenant-uploaded plugin code is accepted or leased. Built-in models keep working. global_spend_cap_micros Once the platform's spend in the current UTC day (or month) reaches the cap, no new compute starts except for internal tenants. Spend counts the cost ledger plus the estimates of work not metered yet: admitted runs at admission, started runs (one by one) at dispatch

Both answer QUOTA_EXCEEDED at the global level. GET /v1/admin/usage returns the spend in the cap's current window next to the cap (spend_cap), and the admin console shows it as a meter that warns at 70% and 90%. In a suspected sandbox escape, turning off untrusted execution is the first step of the incident runbook.

docs.title: Representations and summaries
docs.text:
"One output shape for every model" sounds tidy and is quietly wrong. A conformal interval is not a distribution; per-cell quantiles cannot be added up; a point prediction has no uncertainty to summarise. So every model declares its representation, and the platform uses it to decide which summaries and aggregations it will compute.

Representation Shape Typical models Summaries Aggregate over cells draws (chain, draw, …) joint samples PyMC (MCMC, VI), bootstrap mean, sd, median, hdi_<p>, eti_<p>, q<p> any, per draw quantiles (quantile, …) per cell xgboost / sklearn quantile regression median, q<p>, eti_<p>, point (interpolated, never extrapolated) none interval (bound, …) + alpha split conformal interval, point none point (…) ridge, random forest, classifiers mean, point sum/mean, flagged moments (moment, …) mean and sd analytic Gaussian processes mean, sd, eti_<p>, point none

docs.title: Why aggregation depends on it
docs.text:
With joint draws the total over 40 stores is easy and exact: add the stores within each draw, then summarise. With quantiles you cannot do that: the sum of 40 90% quantiles is not the 90% quantile of the sum (it overstates it, often badly), and the quantiles say nothing about how stores co-vary. Conformal intervals guarantee per-cell coverage only; a "summed interval" would claim a coverage nobody measured.

The rules are data, in mapi_spec, and the summariser and the API both use them:

from mapi_spec import Representation, can_aggregate, default_summary, summary_allowed

for rep in Representation:
    verdict = can_aggregate(rep, ["store"], how="sum")
    print(f"{rep.value:10} sum over stores: {verdict.allowed!s:5} default summary: {default_summary(rep)}")
# draws      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['mean', 'hdi_90']
# quantiles  sum over stores: False default summary: ['median', 'q5', 'q95']
# interval   sum over stores: False default summary: ['point', 'interval']
# point      sum over stores: True  default summary: ['point']
# moments    sum over stores: False default summary: ['mean', 'sd']

print(can_aggregate(Representation.POINT, ["store"]).flagged)  # True: allowed, but labelled
print(can_aggregate(Representation.QUANTILES, ["store"]).reason)
# Quantiles are marginal per cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.
print(summary_allowed(Representation.QUANTILES, "hdi_90"))  # False: no draws to find an HDI
print(summary_allowed(Representation.DRAWS, "q97_5"))  # True

Asking for something the representation cannot support fails before any compute:

CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED - cannot aggregate 'quantiles' output: Quantiles are marginal per
cell; summing quantiles is not a quantile of the sum.

docs.title: Asking for outputs
docs.text:
A score request's output block is an OutputSelector:

output:
  kind: expected              # expected (the mean response) or predictive (with noise)
  summary: [mean, hdi_90]     # default depends on the representation
  draws: 200                  # also return 200 joint draws (draws representation only)
  aggregate: {over: [store]}  # reduce before summarising, if the representation allows
  units: original             # or: model (skip inverse transforms)
  names: dataset              # or: canonical (skip reverse binding)

Summary names are parsed, not looked up: hdi_90, eti_80, q5, q97_5, median, sd. When you leave summary unset you get the representation's default (mean, hdi_90 for draws, median, q5, q95 for quantiles, adapted to the fitted quantile grid).

docs.title: Expected vs predictive
docs.text:
• expected returns the model's mean response (for PyMC models, a Deterministic the plugin names), without observation noise. Use it for "what is the effect of the plan?".
  • predictive returns draws of the observed variable, with noise. Use it for "what range of sales should we plan for?".

docs.title: Draws are thinned once, for the whole bundle
docs.text: When a request asks for draws, they come from a bundle-wide thinning index: the same (chain, draw) pairs for every output and every derived quantity. Contributions, response curves and predictions taken from the same draws stay jointly consistent, so a Guided-mode slider that combines them keeps honest uncertainty bands.

docs.title: Counterfactuals share their noise
docs.text:
In mode: counterfactual the platform scores a baseline and a scenario and returns baseline/ and delta/ groups. Bayesian plugins use common random numbers: the predictive noise of the two runs is the same draw, so the delta reflects the intervention, not two independent noise samples.

Next: Bundles.

docs.title: Security model v0.4
docs.text:
modeling-api is built to run models and data from people it does not trust, from many organisations on one deployment. Every control that does not need a cloud is in the code and tested on a laptop; the cloud controls are written (Terraform, the Cloud Run Jobs executor, Cloud KMS, authenticated Pub/Sub) and tested against fakes, and a short list of cloud behaviours still waits for a real project. This page says what each control protects against, which ones a given executor enforces, and where the honest limits are today.

A local stack is not a security boundary

make dev and Docker Compose run the dev profile: anyone who can reach the API can sign in as any seeded account through the built-in development identity provider. Every port listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose a local stack to a network you do not trust, and do not run untrusted plugin code on it: the local-process and plain docker executors are process isolation, not a multi-tenant boundary.

docs.title: What it protects
docs.text: Asset Threat Main controls Each tenant's data Another tenant, or a bug, reads or changes it PostgreSQL row-level security pinned per transaction and failing closed; storage keys built by the server from ids; roles checked at every request; operators never read tenant content The control plane A hostile dataset, bundle or plot exploits a parser in the API The API parses JSON and YAML only (a strict loader: no anchors or tags, size and depth caps). Arrays, zarr, netCDF, CSV and Parquet are opened only inside a run's sandbox Credentials and other runs Model code reads or steals what the run holds A fresh sandbox per run; supervisor/worker split; no secrets in the environment or arguments; a one-time bootstrap object; object-scoped, short-lived signed URLs Results A run forges outputs, swaps an object later, or fakes progress Outputs are claims checked against the store's own checksums and generations; write-once bundles; signed bundle manifests checked before every download link; HMAC-signed events The bill A leaked token, a runaway sweep or abuse runs up compute vCPU-second quotas per token, tenant and platform; fair-share scheduling; a global spend cap and a kill switch for uploaded code The browser and the user's data A malicious plot spec runs script in the app A server-side sanitizer, then rendering only in a sandboxed iframe on a separate origin, with strict CSPs on both origins; sessions in HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookies with CSRF tokens The user's terminal and screen Log lines or messages with escape codes, HTML or bidi tricks Untrusted text is a separate field (untrusted_text), stripped of ANSI, control and bidi characters, and rendered as text only Long-term trust in a model Pickle and other code-executing formats Bundles are zarr zips plus JSON; native models are skops (allow-listed types) or xgboost JSON; pickle is refused on write and on read

docs.title: Threats, in plain terms
docs.text:
The plan's threat model, as a user would ask about it. Enforced means in the code and covered by tests on every change; [verify M0] means the control is built but depends on a cloud behaviour not yet confirmed against a real Cloud Run Jobs execution (see the checklist).

If someone tries to… What stops them In v0.4 Break out of the sandbox into the machine A fresh microVM per run; the model code runs as its own non-root user with no_new_privs, on a read-only root filesystem Built for Cloud Run Jobs; the uid split there is [verify M0]. Local executors are not boundaries Steal the run's credentials Nothing secret in the environment or arguments; the run's instructions are read from a one-time object and deleted before model code starts; the only credential can get and delete that object, nothing else Enforced (locally the storage emulator enforces the same permissions) Send your data out over the network Deny-all egress, only Google's restricted APIs address, a VPC Service Controls perimeter Terraform written and tested offline; [verify M0] Send your data out over DNS A DNS response policy that answers nothing outside Google APIs [verify M0]. Until it passes, verified and public tenants are not placed on Cloud Run at all Crash or take over the API with a crafted file The API only parses JSON and YAML; everything else is opened inside a sandbox Enforced Swap or replay a model's files Outputs checked against the store's own hashes and generations, copied where runs cannot write, and signed; the signature is checked before every download link Enforced (Cloud KMS signing tested against a fake) Fake progress or results Only the supervisor writes events, each signed and numbered; the executor's own status decides whether a run is alive Enforced Read another organisation's work Row-level security on every table, failing closed; ids checked against the caller's tenant; a test reuses pooled connections across two tenants Enforced Use a leaked token Tokens are scoped, bound to one project, expire, can carry rate limits and budgets, are revoked at once, and never carry operator powers; failed uses are audited Enforced Run up a huge bill, or starve everyone else Quotas in vCPU-seconds per token, tenant and platform; interactive work ahead of batch; a global spend cap; a switch that stops all uploaded code Enforced Run script in your browser through a plot A sanitizer, then a sandboxed iframe on another origin with a strict CSP Enforced Hijack the runner with a malicious package The supervisor runs in its own environment (python -I -S); package uploads are checked for .pth and sitecustomize Supervisor isolation enforced; uploaded packages arrive with the overlay pipeline (v0.5) Slip something into the supply chain Hash-locked Python, digest-pinned images, a frozen JavaScript lockfile without install scripts, keyless CI identities Enforced in the builds; signed-image enforcement (Binary Authorization) comes with public code upload Turn a webhook against your network (SSRF) Static URL checks, one DNS resolution with every address checked, a connection pinned to the checked address, no redirects, time and size caps; private, loopback and link-local addresses and odd ports refused Enforced (to public hosts covered by unit tests; the development allow-list is refused in the multi-tenant profile) Forge or replay a webhook delivery to your receiver An HMAC-SHA256 signature over a timestamp and the raw body under a per-webhook secret shown once and stored sealed; receivers refuse stale timestamps; envelopes carry ids and states, never data, links or secrets Enforced (mapi_client.webhooks.verify) Use an embed link to see more than one chart A tokenised link to one saved plot of a platform recipe, stored as a keyed hash; the public view reads no credential, inlines only that plot's data, is rate-limited per link and per address, and stops on revocation or expiry Enforced Sign up many workspaces to farm free compute E-mail verification, disposable domains refused, per-address, per-domain and platform-wide sign-up limits, Sybil flags reviewed by operators; public workspaces run built-ins and declarative specs only (cut line A), and only on executors that enforce egress and DNS Enforced; vendor identity verification and a public run on such an executor await a deployment Keep a tenant's data after it leaves Tenant deletion purges every table and object prefix after a grace period and notifies by signed webhook; a GDPR export with credentials redacted Enforced; only the pseudonymised audit log and the cost ledger are retained Misuse the MCP server Curated tools with delimited untrusted text Not applicable yet: the MCP server comes in v0.5

The probes that check these rows as hostile code, executor by executor, are the security suite.

docs.title: What each executor enforces
docs.text:
Each executor declares its isolation level and whether it enforces egress and DNS. The dispatcher compares that with the tenant's trust tier before every run, in code: no tenant setting can lower the bar.

Executor Isolation Egress / DNS enforced Tenants it may run Security suite must show inproc NONE No Your own notebook only (never through the API) — local-process PROCESS No internal, self-hosted-trusted. Refuses to start under MAPI_PROFILE=multi-tenant Platform probes BLOCKED; sandbox probes may be ALLOWED docker (runc) PROCESS Only with MAPI_DOCKER_NETWORK=none internal, self-hosted-trusted As above docker-gvisor GVISOR when the supervisor can drop the worker to its own uid, else PROCESS Only with MAPI_DOCKER_NETWORK=none (needs an HTTPS bootstrap URL, so not with the local shim) Every tier once egress and DNS are enforced Every probe BLOCKED cloudrun-jobs MICROVM Egress yes (MAPI_CLOUDRUN_EGRESS_ENFORCED); DNS only once MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED=true, after the M0 DNS check internal, self-hosted-trusted; verified and public once DNS is enforced Every probe BLOCKED, run inside an execution (not wired up yet)

What every executor shares, whatever its isolation: the supervisor/worker protocol, the scrubbed worker environment, capped logs and outputs, HMAC-signed events, and verification of every output by the control plane. What only the stronger levels add is a boundary between the model code and the machine it runs on.

docs.title: Local development vs production
docs.text: Control make dev Docker Compose Google Cloud (v0.3) Authentication The development IdP: any seeded account, no password; 127.0.0.1 only Same; ports published on 127.0.0.1 only OIDC for people (Google or another provider), scoped API tokens with budgets for programs Tenancy Multiple tenants and row-level security, exactly as in production Same Same, on Cloud SQL with separate database logins per role Run isolation A separate worker process with a scrubbed environment, as your own user (DEV_MODE_ISOLATION) local-process: as above, inside a hardened container. docker executor: one container per run, read-only root, no-new-privileges, the supervisor with only the capabilities the uid split needs and the worker as uid 10001 with none (MAPI_REQUIRE_ISOLATION) A fresh Cloud Run Jobs microVM per run; the worker under its own uid with no_new_privs; read-only root Network egress from runs Not restricted docker executor: the GCS shim's network namespace, or an internal network containing only the shim Deny-all egress, including DNS, inside a VPC Service Controls perimeter Object storage permissions The GCS shim enforces per-principal permissions: runs' credentials can only get and delete their bootstrap object Same Cloud Storage IAM; the same layout and principals Bundle signatures EC P-256 with a local key in .local/keys/ EC P-256 with one key on the keys volume, created by migrate and mounted read-only into api and worker Cloud KMS, same signed bytes Event integrity HMAC per event, read from the supervisor's stdout pipe Same HMAC per event, through Cloud Logging and Pub/Sub push with an OIDC token checked by the events service Web app CSP The Vite dev server does not send the app's CSP (hot reload needs inline scripts); the plot sandbox's CSP is enforced Enforced by nginx, with Trusted Types in report-only mode Enforced Plot isolation Separate origin (port 5174), sandbox="allow-scripts" Separate origin (port 5174) Separate domain (plots.<domain>) Quotas and cost limits Tier defaults, quotas, the cost ledger and kill switches all apply Same, plus worker memory, CPU and /tmp limits Same, priced with the deployment's price table

docs.title: The run sandbox
docs.text:
Every run is a pair of processes started by an executor that passes only the run id and a 256-bit nonce. The trusted supervisor uses the nonce to fetch its instructions (signed URLs for its inputs and outputs, an event HMAC key, limits) from a one-time bootstrap object, and deletes it before any model code starts; the storage credential it used can get and delete bootstrap objects and do nothing else, not even list them. The worker that runs the SDK and the plugin gets an allow-listed environment with every MAPI_* variable removed, its own session, and (where the supervisor starts as root) a separate uid with no_new_privs and no core dumps. It can only talk to the supervisor, in schema-checked frames.

On a laptop the supervisor is not root, so the worker runs as you: the run reports DEV_MODE_ISOLATION. Everything else (the split, the scrubbed environment, signed events, caps, output verification) still applies, but the boundary between your account and the model code is only as strong as Python's process separation. Treat local runs like running the plugin in a notebook.

docs.title: Outputs are claims
docs.text: A run can only write under its own attempt prefix, through a POST policy with a size range. When it finishes, the control plane does not read its outputs; it lists them and compares the size, CRC32C, MD5 and generation the store computed with the run's signed manifest. Any missing, changed or extra object fails the run with INTEGRITY_FAILURE and raises an alert. Verified objects are copied server-side into a write-once bundles bucket the runs cannot reach, and a bundle manifest binding the tenant, run, hashes and every destination generation is signed. Download links are minted only after that signature verifies, and each link is pinned to an object generation and expires after 15 minutes. Deleting the signing key (.local/keys/) therefore makes existing model versions undownloadable, by design.

docs.title: Events and liveness
docs.text: Only the supervisor writes the real stdout. Each event line carries a sequence number and an HMAC under the run's key; the control plane verifies it in constant time, deduplicates on (run, attempt, seq) and drops forged lines (counting them as sandbox violations). Events never decide whether a run is alive: the executor's own status does, so a run cannot keep itself "running" by talking, or get itself killed by going quiet.

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
Plot specs come from recipes, plugins and, later, users, and Vega and Plotly are large JavaScript libraries. So:

  1. The server sanitizes every spec when a run finishes and again on every read: pinned Vega-Lite and Plotly schemas, no URL data, no href encodings, no external images, no tile maps, no prototype keys, Plotly HTML reduced to b, i, br, sub, sup, and size and depth caps.
  2. Every plot renders in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> (no allow-same-origin) from the plot sandbox's origin, with default-src 'none', scripts from its own origin only, connect-src limited to its own topojson, and frame-ancestors set to the app.
  3. Vega runs with the expression interpreter (no eval), a loader that rejects every URL and a text-only tooltip; Plotly uses its strict bundle.
  4. The app and the sandbox exchange a small, validated postMessage protocol; the app accepts messages only from that iframe's window with an opaque origin.

The remaining risk (a sandboxed frame could navigate itself and leak the data posted into it) is accepted only for a viewer's own data; shared and embedded plots (v0.4) render platform recipes only.

docs.title: Untrusted text
docs.text: Log lines, tracebacks and plugin messages travel in untrusted_text or LogLine.line, never in detail. The runner strips ANSI, control and bidi characters; the web app renders them as text (ESLint forbids dangerouslySetInnerHTML); Monaco hovers are untrusted; the CLI strips escape sequences before printing.

docs.title: Supply chain
docs.text:
• Python dependencies are locked with hashes in uv.lock; container images are built from the lock with --frozen, and base images are pinned by digest (make docker-pin-check).
  • Build-time guards fail an image that contains what it must not: no numpy, xarray, PyMC, SDK or plugin in the control-plane image, and the import-linter contracts run against the installed packages inside the server image build.
  • The web image installs JavaScript dependencies with --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts.
  • This documentation site's OpenAPI explorer loads a vendored, hash-pinned Redoc bundle; it makes no request outside the site.

docs.title: Known gaps in v0.4
docs.text:
• Cloud behaviours not yet verified. Everything marked [verify M0] above, chiefly that the DNS response policy applies to Cloud Run Jobs. Until it is confirmed, the executor declares DNS as not enforced and shared tiers are not placed on it.
  • The nightly security suite does not run in the cloud yet. The probes run locally and against gVisor; the base images do not ship them and Terraform defines no probe Job (Security suite).
  • Executor conformance reports are not stored, so the admin console shows every executor as conformance not passed and enabling an executor is not gated on a stored report (M2 verification). Placement by trust tier is enforced regardless.
  • Identity Platform's own tokens are not accepted by the browser sign-in yet; use Google or another OpenID provider (Authentication).
  • Public workspaces need an enforcing executor. Sign-up creates public workspaces, which run only on docker-gvisor or on Cloud Run Jobs once its DNS enforcement is verified; a deployment with neither cannot run their work. Neither ran in the M3 verification (what remains).
  • Identity verification has no vendor integration yet: operators verify tenants by hand (audited), behind the IdentityVerifier protocol.
  • Webhook deliveries to the internet were exercised only through the development allow-list; the SSRF policy for public hosts is covered by unit tests.
  • The API's built-in /docs and /redoc pages (FastAPI's defaults) load Swagger UI and Redoc from a public CDN. Use the OpenAPI explorer or /openapi.json instead.
  • The app's CSP is not enforced by the Vite dev server (see the table).
  • Under the local-process executor, run code runs as the orchestrator's own uid, so it can read the shim's control key and the bundle-signing key. The orchestrator is non-dumpable and logs a warning at start-up, but run only trusted plugin code in this mode; see Docker Compose.

docs.title: What comes next
docs.text: Plugin upload for allow-listed teams comes in v0.5, built into hash-pinned overlays and checked by the contract kit on upload. Public code upload (every tenant uploading their own plugins) comes only after a dedicated overlay build pipeline with a curated package mirror, a separate execution project for public tenants, Binary Authorization on base images, abuse controls (verification before any code runs), a rehearsed kill-switch drill and an external penetration test, with the security suite green in the cloud for two weeks.

docs.title: Tenancy and authentication v0.3
docs.text:
From v0.3 one deployment serves many organisations. Each is a tenant; inside it, work is organised in projects; people and programs get roles in projects. Every request is authenticated (who is calling), scoped (in which project) and authorized (may they do this), by one pure function that the API, the web app and the tests share. The contracts live in mapi_spec.tenancy and mapi_spec.tokens; the endpoints are listed in HTTP API: Multi-tenant API.

Coming from v0.2

A v0.2 install had one tenant and one project, both called default, and no sign-in. Every row and storage key already carried the tenant and project, so v0.3 needs no data migration: your work is in default/default. MAPI_PROFILE=single-tenant keeps the old credential-less behaviour. The practical side of this page (who does what, with screenshots and a tested walkthrough) is the Administration guide; signing in is Authentication.

docs.title: Tenants and projects
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    T["Tenant <b>acme</b><br/>trust tier · status · data residency<br/><i>billing, isolation and quota boundary</i>"]
    T --> P1["Project <b>growth</b><br/>datasets · specs · runs · models"]
    T --> P2["Project <b>retail</b>"]
    U1(["Ana: runner in growth"]) -.-> P1
    U2(["IT: admin of acme (tenant-wide)"]) -.-> T
    K(["token mapi_7k2m…: bound to growth"]) -.-> P1

A tenant is the unit of billing, isolation and quotas. Postgres enforces it with row-level security on tenant_id in every table, and every storage key starts with t/{tenant}/. A tenant has:

Field Values Effect Trust tier internal, verified, public, self-hosted-trusted Where its runs may execute, and its default quotas Status active, suspended, deleting suspended tenants can read but not change or run anything; deleting tenants are inaccessible Data residency A multi-region (eu, us, asia) or one region (europe-west1) Runs go only to executors that declare a matching region (Cloud Run Jobs declare theirs). The self-hosted executors (local-process, docker, docker-gvisor) declare no region and are not checked: there the install's location is the residency

The trust tier decides placement. This is enforced by the dispatcher, never by tenant configuration:

Tier Who Executor must provide internal The platform team Process isolation or better self-hosted-trusted A single organisation running its own install Process isolation or better verified Known customers (identity or card verified) gVisor or a microVM, with egress and DNS enforced public Anyone who signed up gVisor or a microVM, with egress and DNS enforced

So a verified or public tenant's runs never land on the local-process or plain docker executor. The executor must also have passed the executor conformance suite and the security suite for its current configuration, recorded by an operator (the shared-tier gate). Until an executor qualifies, those tenants' runs are refused at submission. New tenants are verified by default.

A project is a workspace inside a tenant and the unit of access control. Its id is a short slug, unique in the tenant, because it appears in references such as dataset://growth/eu_media_daily.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
There are four project roles. Each includes everything the one before it can do:

Role Can viewer Read everything in the project: datasets, specs, runs, logs, models, plots, usage. Validate specs. Mint tokens for themselves. editor Also create and change datasets, specs and saved plots. runner Also spend compute: submit, cancel, resume and retry runs; score models and endpoints; render plots. admin Also manage members, endpoints and their promotion, plugins, other people's tokens, and delete things.

Running sits above editing on purpose: compute costs money, so a teammate can be trusted to edit a spec without being able to start a 200-task sweep.

A membership grants one role, either on one project or tenant-wide. A tenant-wide grant applies to the tenant itself (renaming it, its member list, its audit log and bill) and to every project in it. In a project, a member's effective role is the higher of their tenant-wide and project grants.

The complete permission matrix is mapi_spec.tenancy.PERMISSIONS. A test checks every role, action and resource combination against an independently written table. In summary:

Resource read create update delete Other tenant viewer (tenant-wide) operator admin (tenant-wide) operator manage (tier, status, residency): operator tenant members viewer (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) admin (tenant-wide) — project viewer admin (tenant-wide) admin admin (tenant-wide) — project members viewer admin admin admin — token viewer viewer — viewer (own) manage (others' tokens): admin catalog viewer — — — — dataset, spec viewer editor editor admin — run viewer runner — — cancel: runner model viewer — — admin run (score): runner endpoint viewer admin admin admin run: runner; promote: admin plot viewer editor — — run (render): runner plugin viewer admin — admin — usage (project) viewer — — — — billing, audit (tenant) admin (tenant-wide) — — — — quotas, kill switches, executors operator — operator operator —

Operators run the platform. They manage tenants, quotas, kill switches and executors, and can read tenant metadata, usage and audit logs. They cannot read tenant content (datasets, specs, models, plots) through the API: no role or flag grants that.

from mapi_spec.tenancy import Action, ProjectRole, ResourceKind, can

print(can(ProjectRole.EDITOR, Action.UPDATE, ResourceKind.SPEC))  # True
print(can(ProjectRole.EDITOR, Action.CREATE, ResourceKind.RUN))  # False: running costs money
print(can(ProjectRole.RUNNER, Action.CREATE, ResourceKind.RUN))  # True
print(can(ProjectRole.ADMIN, Action.UPDATE, ResourceKind.KILL_SWITCH))  # False: operators only

docs.title: Who can call
docs.text: Principal How it authenticates Identity User Signs in with OpenID Connect in the browser (issuer, subject) from the identity provider, mapped to a platform id usr_… at first sign-in Token Authorization: Bearer mapi_… The token id tok_…; it acts as its owner, a user or a service account sa_… (a service token) Internal service Platform identity (for example, Pub/Sub's signed OIDC token on /internal/events) svc_…; only internal routes accept it

docs.title: How a request is authorized
docs.text:
1. Authenticate. A session cookie, a bearer token or a service identity. Missing or invalid: 401 UNAUTHENTICATED.
  2. Select the project. From the path, the X-Mapi-Project: <tenant>/<project> header, or the token's binding (see below).
  3. Resolve roles. The caller's tenant-wide and project roles, from memberships now. For a token, its owner's memberships: removing a person from a project immediately disarms their tokens there.
  4. Check the permission. AuthContext.allows(action, resource) applies, in order: internal rules, operator rules, the tenant's status, the role at the rule's level and, for tokens, the scopes. A resource the caller cannot see answers 404; a visible one they may not change answers 403 FORBIDDEN.
  5. Check quotas before anything that consumes compute or storage (see Quotas and cost).
from mapi_spec.tenancy import AuthContext, TenantStatus, TokenPrincipal

token = TokenPrincipal(
    id="tok_01jaf3r1s2t3v4w5x6y7z8a9b0",
    prefix="7k2m9q4x",
    owner_id="usr_01jaf3a9b8c7d6e5f4g3h2j1k0",
    tenant_id="acme",
    project_id="growth",
    scopes=("score:geo-mmm-prod",),
)
ctx = AuthContext(
    principal=token,
    tenant_id="acme",
    project_id="growth",
    role=ProjectRole.ADMIN,  # the owner's role in the project, resolved now
    scopes=frozenset(token.scopes),
)
print(ctx.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # True
print(ctx.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="other"))  # False: not in the scopes
print(ctx.allows("read", "dataset"))  # False: scopes narrow even an admin's token

frozen = ctx.model_copy(update={"tenant_status": TenantStatus.SUSPENDED})
print(frozen.allows("read", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # True: reads still work
print(frozen.allows("run", "endpoint", resource_name="geo-mmm-prod"))  # False

docs.title: Selecting the project
docs.text:
Every resource of v0.2 (datasets, specs, runs, models, plots) now lives in a project. Send X-Mapi-Project: acme/growth, or a bare X-Mapi-Project: growth when the tenant is unambiguous. Tokens are bound to one project and may omit the header; naming another project with a token is 403 FORBIDDEN. A local single-tenant install falls back to default/default.

Because a token is bound to one project, it cannot administer its tenant: tenant members, creating or deleting projects, the tenant audit log and tenant usage need a signed-in session (403 FORBIDDEN for any token, whatever its scopes and its owner's role). A token may still read its own tenant (GET /v1/tenants/{tenant}) and list its own project.

from mapi_spec.tenancy import resolve_project_scope

print(resolve_project_scope(header="acme/growth"))  # acme/growth
print(resolve_project_scope(header="growth", member_tenants=["acme"]))  # acme/growth
print(resolve_project_scope(token_binding=("acme", "growth")))  # acme/growth

docs.title: API tokens
docs.text:
Programs (the Python client, the CLI, Atlas, BI exports) use API tokens:

mapi_7k2m9q4x_0123456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstvwxyz072gj7d
     prefix   secret (160 random bits)        checksum
  • Lowercase Crockford base32 (no i, l, o, u), so tokens survive being read aloud or retyped.
  • The prefix is public. Listings show the token as mapi_7k2m9q4x_….
  • The secret is shown once, in the response to POST /v1/tokens. The server stores only an HMAC-SHA256 of the whole token under a server-side pepper, and compares in constant time.
  • The checksum (CRC-32 of the rest) lets clients and secret scanners reject typos and random strings without asking the server. Every single-character typo and every swap of two neighbouring characters is caught.
from mapi_spec.errors import MapiError
from mapi_spec.tokens import generate_token, hash_token, parse_token, verify_token_hash

tok = generate_token()
text = str(tok)  # mapi_<8-char prefix>_<32-char secret><7-char checksum>
print(text.startswith("mapi_"), len(text))  # True 53
print(tok.display)  # mapi_<prefix>_…: the only form ever shown again

stored = hash_token(tok, pepper=b"server-side pepper")  # all the server keeps
print(verify_token_hash(text, stored, pepper=b"server-side pepper"))  # True

typo = text[:-1] + ("0" if text[-1] != "0" else "1")
try:
    parse_token(typo)
except MapiError as err:
    print(err.code.value)  # UNAUTHENTICATED: the checksum catches it without a lookup

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A token's scopes narrow what it may do; they never add to its owner's role. An admin's token with models:read can only read.

Scope Allows models:read Read datasets, specs, runs, models, endpoints, plots, usage and the catalog runs:create models:read, plus submit and cancel runs, score models and endpoints, render plots score:{target} Score one model by its id, for example score:mdl_01jaf3r1s2t3v4w5x6y7z8a9b0 (POST /v1/models/{id}/versions/{v}:score); score:* covers every model in the project. Once endpoints exist, an endpoint alias works the same way, for example score:geo-mmm-prod datasets:write Create datasets and add versions plugins:publish Publish and yank plugins (from v0.5) admin Everything the owner's role allows, except minting tokens

No scope lets a token mint tokens: a child token would escape its parent's expiry, budget, rate limit and revocation. Mint tokens from a signed-in session (mapi login or the browser).

Each token also has an expiry (default 90 days, at most 365), and may have its own requests-per-minute limit and a vCPU-second budget per day or month. These apply in addition to the tenant's quotas.

docs.title: Signing in from the browser
docs.text:
The web app never holds an OAuth token. The API acts as a backend-for-frontend:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant A as API (/auth)
    participant I as Identity provider
    B->>A: GET /auth/login?return_to=/runs
    A->>A: new state, nonce, PKCE verifier (kept server-side, 10 min)
    A-->>B: 302 to IdP (code_challenge S256, state, nonce) + __Host-mapi_login cookie
    B->>I: sign in
    I-->>B: 302 /auth/callback?code&state
    B->>A: GET /auth/callback (with the login cookie)
    A->>I: exchange code + PKCE verifier
    I-->>A: ID token
    A->>A: check issuer, audience, nonce, expiry; map (issuer, subject) to usr_…
    A-->>B: 302 /runs + __Host-mapi_session (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict)
    B->>A: fetch /v1/... (cookie sent same-site only)
  • The session cookie is HttpOnly (scripts cannot read it), Secure, SameSite=Strict (cross-site requests never carry it) and host-only (__Host- prefix: no Domain, Path=/).
  • Sessions end after 2 hours idle or 12 hours in total. POST /auth/logout ends one at once.
  • State-changing requests made with the session cookie also carry the session's CSRF token in X-CSRF-Token (from the readable __Host-mapi_csrf cookie or GET /auth/session); without it, or from another origin, they are refused.
  • return_to only accepts a path on the same origin, so the login flow cannot be used as an open redirect.
  • GET /auth/session tells the web app whether it is signed in (authenticated: false is a normal 200 answer).

docs.title: Audit
docs.text: Security-relevant actions are written to an append-only audit log: sign-ins, token creation and revocation, membership and project changes, quota and kill-switch changes, artifact link minting, quota denials and rejected run events. Each entry records the actor's platform id, the action, the resource, the outcome and a problem code. Client IP addresses and user agents are stored only as keyed HMACs, so entries can be correlated without being reversible. Tenant admins read their tenant's log at GET /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/audit; operators read everything at GET /v1/admin/audit.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
There are three ways in, and they share everything: the spec format, the steps, the models and the bundles.

  • Guided mode, no code v0.4

    For analysts: pick a template, upload a spreadsheet, answer a few questions and get a report, a sanity scorecard and what-if sliders. Needs a running platform: your team's, or make dev below.

    Your first MMM in Guided mode

  • Run the platform v0.2

    Start the API, the job queue, the sandboxed runner and the web app on your laptop with make dev, then fit and score from the browser, the CLI, Python or HTTP.

    Quickstart: zero to first model in 10 minutes

  • Use the library in your own process

    import mapi_sdk in a notebook, a script or a test suite: validate specs, fit, score and write bundles in-process, and test your own plugins with the contract kit.

    Your first model in Python

Both need Python 3.12 and uv. The platform also needs Node.js 22+ with pnpm for the web app; Docker is optional (Deployment).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From a clone (today)Into your own project (once published)

The packages are developed together in one uv workspace. Clone the repository and sync every package plus the developer tools:

git clone <repository-url> modeling-api
cd modeling-api
uv sync --all-packages        # or: make install (also installs the web app)
uv run python -c "import mapi_sdk, mapi_spec; print(mapi_sdk.__version__)"

Open a notebook in the same environment with uv run --with jupyterlab jupyter lab.

Each package is a separate distribution, so you install only what you need:

uv add mapi-sdk mapi-steps                 # the runtime and the built-in steps
uv add mapi-pymc                           # PyMC models
uv add mapi-sklearn                        # scikit-learn and xgboost models
uv add "mapi-plots[recipes]"               # plot recipes (Altair, Plotly)
uv add mapi-plugin-mmm mapi-plugin-ts mapi-plugin-tabular   # the built-in models

Not on PyPI yet

The distributions are published with the first tagged release. Until then, install from the workspace as shown in the first tab.

docs.title: What each package does
docs.text:
Package Import What it gives you Heavy dependencies mapi-spec mapi_spec The contracts: DataSchema, ModelSpec, ScoreRequest, capabilities, error codes, static validation, JSON Schemas none (pure Pydantic) mapi-sdk mapi_sdk The runtime: steps, pipelines, coord plans, summaries, bundles, the in-process executor and the contract kit xarray, numpy, zarr mapi-steps mapi_steps 28 built-in preprocessing steps and the split catalog – mapi-pymc mapi_pymc PyMCModel: write build(), get engines, diagnostics, new levels and counterfactuals PyMC mapi-sklearn mapi_sklearn SklearnModel: write estimator(), get stacking, safe persistence and uncertainty scikit-learn, xgboost, skops mapi-plots mapi_plots The JSON-only plot sanitizer and templates; recipes with the recipes extra Altair, Plotly (extra) mapi-plugin-* mapi_plugin_* Built-in models: marketing mix, time series, tabular as above mapi-conformance mapi_conformance The conformance corpus and its runner all of the above mapi-client mapi_client Typed Python client for the HTTP API (guide) httpx (xarray optional) mapi-cli mapi_cli The mapi command line (guide) typer, rich mapi-server mapi_server The control plane: API, orchestrator, executors (AGPL or commercial) FastAPI, SQLAlchemy; no numpy mapi-runner mapi_runner The sandboxed run harness: supervisor and worker (AGPL or commercial) the SDK, in the worker only mapi-gcs-shim mapi_gcs_shim A local emulator of the Cloud Storage features the platform uses Starlette

Plugins register themselves through Python entry points (mapi.steps, mapi.models, mapi.plots), so mapi_sdk.default_registry() finds everything that is installed.

docs.title: Runs and executors
docs.text:
fit_spec and score_bundle are plain functions. The platform does the same work as runs: JSON-only submissions handed to an executor, which reports progress as events and returns a status that is the source of truth. The in-process executor implements that protocol inside your Python process, so notebooks, tests and the platform's local-process and docker executors share one code path.

sequenceDiagram
    participant You as Notebook / API
    participant Ex as Executor
    participant H as Harness (fit_spec / score_bundle)
    You->>Ex: submit(RunSubmit{kind: fit, payload: spec}, nonce)
    Ex->>H: resolve dataset refs, fit
    H-->>Ex: progress events
    Ex-->>You: event stream (state, progress, complete)
    You->>Ex: wait(handle) → SUCCEEDED
    You->>Ex: submit(RunSubmit{kind: score, payload: request + bundle})
    Ex->>H: score_bundle
    Ex-->>You: result: xr.DataTree

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
The executor resolves the dataset:// references in specs and requests through a resolver. Here it is a mapping to in-memory datasets; the built-in tabular plugin ships the store-demand data and spec used below.

import asyncio

from mapi_plugin_tabular.datasets import (
    STORE_DEMAND_SCHEMA,
    STORE_DEMAND_SPEC_YAML,
    store_demand_dataset,
)
from mapi_sdk import InprocExecutor
from mapi_spec.executor import ExecState, RunEventType, RunKind, RunSubmit

history = store_demand_dataset(stores=4, skus=2, weeks=60, seed=1)
recent = history.isel(week=slice(-8, None))  # a window of fitted weeks to re-score

executor = InprocExecutor(
    # dataset refs in specs and requests resolve to in-memory datasets
    resolver={
        "dataset://retail/store_sku_weekly@latest": history,
        "dataset://retail/last_8_weeks@v1": recent,
    },
)
print(executor.caps().isolation.name)  # NONE: your own code, in your own process

docs.title: Submit, wait, score
docs.text:
async def main() -> None:
    fit = await executor.submit(
        RunSubmit(
            run_id="fit-001",
            kind=RunKind.FIT,
            payload={
                "spec": STORE_DEMAND_SPEC_YAML,
                "raw_schema": STORE_DEMAND_SCHEMA.model_dump(mode="json"),
            },
        ),
        nonce="nonce-fit-0001",  # resubmitting the same nonce returns the same run
    )
    status = await executor.wait(fit, timeout=300)
    print(status.state)  # succeeded
    for event in executor.events(fit):  # the same event stream a cloud run will produce
        if event.type is RunEventType.PROGRESS:
            print(event.seq, event.payload.get("message"))  # 2 validated the spec and the data

    executor.put_bundle("store-demand@1", executor.result(fit))
