The executor also sets MAPI_REQUIRE_ISOLATION=1, which makes the supervisor fail the run with SANDBOX_VIOLATION rather than run the worker under its own uid.

Neither mode is a multi-tenant boundary. Both are single-tenant local stacks, and the local-process executor refuses any multi-tenant profile.

What a local-process run can reach. Every run is a subprocess of mapi-server worker and runs as the same uid, 10001. There is no uid split before v0.3. Run code, meaning plugins and the steps they load, can therefore read everything the orchestrator can read:

  • the shim's control key (/shim/gcs/_shim/keys/control.json): storage.admin on every bucket, enough to read or rewrite bundles, datasets and run outputs and to mint signed URLs;
  • the bundle-signing key (/var/lib/mapi/keys/), enough to forge a manifest the API accepts;
  • the executions directory under /tmp/mapi-data, including the pid files that name the nonces of runs in flight.

In this mode, then, bundle signatures and the finalizer's output checks protect against accidents, not against hostile plugin code. The orchestrator marks itself non-dumpable, so run code cannot ptrace it or read its /proc/<pid>/environ (DATABASE_URL with the password) or its memory. The worker also logs this warning at start-up. Run only trusted plugin code under local-process. The docker executor does not have this exposure: each attempt runs in its own container with none of these files mounted. The worker's /tmp is the scratch space for local-process runs. Size it with MAPI_WORKER_TMPFS, MAPI_WORKER_MEMORY and MAPI_WORKER_CPUS in .env.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Compose reads .env in the repository root (copy .env.example). POSTGRES_PASSWORD is required; the MAPI_WORKER_* sizes, the image version (MAPI_VERSION, set by the Makefile) and the web image's MAPI_API_UPSTREAM and MAPI_WEB_SCRIPT_SRC_EXTRA are optional. Every variable is in the configuration reference.

compose.override.example.yml shows the two common changes: publishing PostgreSQL on the host, and switching the worker to the docker executor. Copy it to compose.override.yml (ignored by version control) to use it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: A missing Docker daemon, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, an unhealthy api container, a read-only /tmp and ports that are already allocated are covered in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Deploy to Google Cloud v0.3
docs.text:
This page takes an environment (dev, staging or prod) from empty Google Cloud projects to a running, multi-tenant platform: the API and web app on Cloud Run, runs executing as Cloud Run Jobs in a zero-egress sandbox project, and data in private buckets behind a VPC Service Controls perimeter. Everything is in infra/terraform and driven by four scripts in deploy/gcp.

Status: written, validated and tested offline; not yet applied

The Terraform passes terraform validate for every environment and a terraform test suite that applies every module against mocked providers (see Testing the infrastructure). It has not been applied to a real organisation yet. The server's cloud adapters (Cloud Run Jobs executor, Cloud Storage, KMS signing, Pub/Sub push verification) ship in the same release and are tested against fakes only; the environment variables they read are listed below. Read the next section before you start.

docs.title: Before you start: the [verify M0] checklist
docs.text:
The design rests on cloud behaviours that the documentation of Google Cloud suggests but that nobody has yet confirmed against a real Cloud Run Jobs execution. The plan marks each one [verify M0]. Nothing here is broken by them in a dev environment, but do not admit untrusted tenants until each one has a recorded pass. The full procedure, with the probe for each item, is the M0 verification checklist; the steps that remain after the offline M2 verification are in M2 verification.

Assumption What depends on it If it does not hold The Direct VPC egress resolver honours the DNS response policy (*. to NXDOMAIN, Google APIs to the restricted VIP) DNS exfiltration is blocked; MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED may be set to true, which is what lets verified and public tenants run at all Cloud Run Jobs cannot host untrusted code. Keep shared tiers off it; fall back to GKE Sandbox behind the same executor protocol Deny-all egress and VPC Service Controls apply to Jobs executions Runs cannot reach the internet or buckets outside the perimeter Same as above gen2 allows the supervisor/worker uid split with no_new_privs, seccomp and no ptrace The worker cannot read the supervisor's credentials Runs report DEV_MODE_ISOLATION; the runner images must start the supervisor as root for the split Execution overrides are env-only (no image, resources, service account or network) jobs.run can pass only the run id and nonce The dispatcher's role must be narrowed further The in-memory filesystem limits behave as planned (no ephemeral disk; exit 137 at the limit) Scratch budgets of 3/6/12 GiB for classes S/M/L; RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED with a retry one class up Large-data fits move to GKE A deleted bootstrap object cannot be restored The nonce in the audit log points at nothing Terraform already sets the bootstrap bucket's soft-delete window to 0; if a copy can still be restored, the bootstrap design needs a second look before launch Quotas: 180 jobs.run per minute and 1,000 running executions per region The dispatcher's token bucket (150 a minute by default) and the global limit of 700 concurrent runs Lower MAPI_CLOUDRUN_SUBMITS_PER_MINUTE, shard across exec projects Cold start of a ~2.5 GB base image keeps time-to-RUNNING p95 under 90 s The M2 latency target (met offline against the fake backend only) Slimmer images, or warm capacity (M6) The Logging sink to Pub/Sub path carries the execution's labels within seconds, and Pub/Sub can push to an internal-only service Run events and progress Runs still finish (the executor's status decides liveness), but progress goes quiet Cloud SQL managed connection pooling works in transaction mode with the server's driver, and the migrate role can grant BYPASSRLS Row-level security for requests; the platform role for the orchestrator Give mapi_orchestrator its own policy-based access (the explicit policy already exists) run.jobs.runWithOverrides works without iam.serviceAccounts.actAs on the execution account The orchestrator's least-privilege role Grant actAs on that one account Cloud Run accepts the image indexes build-push.sh pushes (with attestations) Deploys Build with --no-attestations

Two further limits of v0.3 are not cloud facts but matter on day one: browser sign-in uses an OpenID provider with an authorization-code endpoint (Google by default; Identity Platform's own tokens are not accepted yet, see Authentication), and the nightly security suite has no probe Job in Terraform yet (Security suite).

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
One environment spans five kinds of project, one per trust zone (plan §8.1):

flowchart TB
    users(("browsers ·<br/>clients")) -->|HTTPS| lb["global HTTPS load balancer<br/>app.example.com · plots.example.net"]
    subgraph control["control project (trusted)"]
        lb --> api["api<br/>Cloud Run"]
        lb --> web["web · plots<br/>Cloud Run"]
        events["events<br/>Cloud Run, internal"]
        orch["orchestrator<br/>worker pool"]
        sql[("Cloud SQL<br/>PostgreSQL 16")]
        kms["KMS<br/>bundle signing"]
        topic["Pub/Sub<br/>run events"]
        api --> sql
        orch --> sql
        events --> sql
        topic -->|"push + OIDC"| events
    end
    subgraph perimeter["VPC-SC perimeter"]
        subgraph exec["exec-paid · exec-public (hostile)"]
            jobs["Cloud Run Jobs<br/>3 bases × S/M/L<br/>deny-all egress"]
            sink["Logging sink<br/>mapi_event lines"]
        end
        subgraph data["data project"]
            buckets[("quarantine · bootstrap · runs<br/>bundles · data")]
        end
    end
    subgraph build["build project"]
        ar["Artifact Registry<br/>images · curated PyPI"]
    end
    orch -->|"jobs.run (env: run id, nonce)"| jobs
    jobs -->|"signed URLs only<br/>(restricted VIP)"| buckets
    jobs --> sink -->|Publish| topic
    jobs -. pull .-> ar
Module Project Creates control control Cloud Run api, events, web, plots; orchestrator worker pool; migrate job; Cloud SQL (private IP, managed connection pooling); Secret Manager secrets; Pub/Sub topic, push subscription and dead letters; one Logging sink per exec project; KMS signing key; Identity Platform; optional load balancer exec each exec project VPC without a default route, deny-all egress firewall, restricted-VIP route and DNS zone, DNS response policy, the Job inventory, the execution service account, the dispatcher role data data The five buckets of plan §8.6 with lifecycle rules, retention, CORS and bucket-level IAM build build Docker repository (immutable tags), curated PyPI remote, Binary Authorization attestor (stub), GitHub Workload Identity Federation perimeter organisation The VPC-SC perimeter around the exec and data projects stack all Wires the modules together and enables the APIs

envs/<env>/main.tf holds each environment's policy (database size and availability, deletion protection, retention lock, perimeter mode) where code review sees it; terraform.tfvars holds only names and ids.

dev staging prod Database Enterprise, 1 vCPU, zonal, no pooler Enterprise Plus, zonal, pooler Enterprise Plus, regional (HA), pooler VPC-SC perimeter dry-run (optional) enforced, required enforced, required Load balancer + domains optional optional required Deletion protection off on on Bundle retention 1 day, unlocked 7 days, unlocked 30 days, locked Signing key software software HSM Minimum instances (api) 0 1 2

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An organisation with an Access Context Manager policy (gcloud access-context-manager policies list --organization ORG_ID). Without one, only dev can be deployed, without the perimeter (every plan then warns).
  • Projects, created by your organisation's project vending: control, data, build, and one exec project per pool (exec-paid, plus exec-public once public tenants exist), all linked to billing. Keep the exec projects free of anything else.
  • Tools: Terraform ≥ 1.11 (tested with 1.14), gcloud, Docker with buildx, python3 and curl.
  • Permissions for the first run: project owner (or equivalent) on every project, and roles/accesscontextmanager.policyEditor on the organisation policy. Later runs use the CI identities Terraform creates.
  • An OAuth client (web application) for the app origin, for browser sign-in.

docs.title: 1. Bootstrap the projects
docs.text:
deploy/gcp/bootstrap.sh --env staging --region europe-west4 \
  --control-project acme-mapi-stg-control --data-project acme-mapi-stg-data \
  --build-project acme-mapi-stg-build \
  --exec-project paid=acme-mapi-stg-exec-paid --exec-project public=acme-mapi-stg-exec-public \
  --state-project acme-mapi-stg-build --dry-run       # read what it will do, then drop --dry-run

It enables each project's APIs (the same lists as modules/stack/apis.tf; a test keeps them identical), creates the state bucket (uniform access, public access prevention, object versioning) and writes infra/terraform/envs/staging/backend.hcl.

docs.title: 2. Describe the environment
docs.text:
cp infra/terraform/envs/staging/terraform.tfvars.example infra/terraform/envs/staging/terraform.tfvars
$EDITOR infra/terraform/envs/staging/terraform.tfvars

Fill in the project ids, region, bucket location (follow your tenants' data residency), the exec pools, the access policy id, the domains, the OAuth client id and the GitHub repository. The file holds no secrets and is not committed.

Data residency and the exec region

A run is placed only on an executor whose region satisfies its tenant's data residency. The default residency (the platform tenant's, and that of every tenant created without one) is therefore what the dispatch pool's region satisfies: eu for europe-west4. Override it with the control module's default_residency. A tenant whose residency the exec region cannot satisfy has its runs refused at submission (403, "no executor of this platform can run this tenant's work"), and the worker logs a warning for it at start-up. Change it with PATCH /v1/admin/tenants/{id} (data_residency).

docs.title: 3. Apply the foundation
docs.text:
deploy/gcp/deploy.sh --env staging --foundation

A foundation apply creates everything except the Cloud Run workloads and Jobs, which need images: the registry, networks, DNS policy, database, secrets, buckets, perimeter and CI identities. deploy.sh always shows the plan and asks you to type the environment name before applying it.

Database passwords, the token pepper and the session key are generated during this apply by ephemeral resources and written with write-only arguments: they are in Secret Manager and nowhere else (not in the state, not in the plan file).

docs.title: 4. Add the OAuth client secret
docs.text:
export TF_VAR_oidc_client_secret='...'      # from the OAuth client
# in terraform.tfvars: oidc_client_secret_version = 1

The secret is an ephemeral Terraform variable: it is written to Secret Manager as a new version and never stored. Raise oidc_client_secret_version whenever you rotate it. Add the identity providers you want to Identity Platform (console, or google_identity_platform_*_idp_config resources outside this module).

docs.title: 5. Build and push the images
docs.text:
deploy/gcp/build-push.sh --env staging

It builds server, web, base-bayes, base-ml and base-forecast for linux/amd64, pushes them as <version>-<git sha> (tags are immutable in the registry, so re-running for the same commit reuses what is there) and writes their digests to deploy/gcp/.out/staging/images.tfvars.json. Terraform refuses any image that is not pinned by digest.

docs.title: 6. Deploy the release
docs.text:
deploy/gcp/deploy.sh --env staging
  1. terraform plan with terraform.tfvars and the images file, saved to a plan file.
  2. Confirmation (type the environment name; --yes skips it in automation).
  3. Migrations first: the mapi-staging-migrate job is pointed at the new server image and executed (deploy/gcp/migrate.sh). Migrations are expand/contract, so the release still serving keeps working on the new schema. On the very first release the job does not exist yet, so they run right after the apply instead.
  4. terraform apply of exactly the saved plan.
  5. The images file is recorded as a release in gs://<state bucket>/mapi/staging/releases/<UTC timestamp>-<release id>.json. The release id is a hash of the images, so a retried deploy of the same images is the same release.
  6. Smoke test: API /healthz and /readyz, the web app (with a Content-Security-Policy), the plot sandbox, and a check that the events service refuses requests from the internet.

docs.title: 7. Point DNS at the load balancer
docs.text:
terraform -chdir=infra/terraform/envs/staging output lb_ip

Create A records for both domains. The Google-managed certificate provisions once DNS resolves (often 15–60 minutes); until then run deploy.sh --skip-smoke. Without domains, the services answer on their run.app URLs (terraform output urls).

docs.title: 8. Verify the controls
docs.text:
Work through the security hardening page, and the M0 verification checklist before the first production deploy. Once the DNS item has a recorded pass, tell the orchestrator so, in the environment's main.tf, and deploy again:

control = {
  # ...
  extra_env = {
    orchestrator = { MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED = "true" }
  }
}

Until then the executor declares DNS as not enforced, and the dispatcher refuses to place verified and public tenants on it (trust tiers).

docs.title: 9. Name the operators and create the first tenant
docs.text:
Platform operators are the people whose verified e-mail is in MAPI_OPERATOR_EMAILS. Set it on the API (plain values only; never secrets in extra_env):

control = {
  # ...
  extra_env = {
    api = { MAPI_OPERATOR_EMAILS = "oncall@acme.example,platform@acme.example" }
  }
}

After deploy/gcp/deploy.sh --env staging, an operator signs in to the web app (or with mapi login --issuer https://accounts.google.com --client-id <the CLI's client id>) and creates each organisation's tenant with its first admin, who is invited by e-mail and becomes tenant admin at their first sign-in:

mapi admin tenants create acme --name "Acme Retail" --tier verified --residency eu \
    --admin-email it@acme.example

From there the tenant admin creates projects and invites people (Administration). Check the platform with the observability dashboards, and import the alerts before you let anyone in.

Verified tenants cannot run until DNS enforcement is verified

verified (the default tier of new tenants, the private beta) and public tenants need an executor with egress and DNS enforced. A fresh stack sets neither MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED nor any suite evidence, so their runs are refused at submission (INFRA_ERROR, 503) and only internal and self_hosted_trusted tenants run. To open the shared tiers:

  1. pass the DNS red-team gate of the M0 checklist from a Job of this environment;
  2. set MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED = "true" for the orchestrator through control.extra_env ({ orchestrator = { MAPI_CLOUDRUN_DNS_ENFORCED = "true" } }) and deploy;
  3. run the executor conformance suite and the security suite against the deployed executor and record both with PUT /v1/admin/executors/cloudrun-jobs/evidence (the shared-tier gate). Evidence expires after MAPI_EXECUTOR_EVIDENCE_MAX_AGE_S, so record the nightly runs.

docs.title: Continuous deployment
docs.text:
.github/workflows/deploy.yml deploys on manual dispatch only, without service-account keys:

Job GitHub environment Google identity Does build <env>-build mapi-<env>-ci-push build-push.sh; uploads the images file plan <env>-plan mapi-<env>-planner (read-only) deploy.sh --plan-only; the plan goes to the job summary apply <env> mapi-<env>-deployer deploy.sh --apply-plan: migrations, apply of that plan, release record, smoke test

Set up, per environment:

  1. Create the three GitHub environments and put required reviewers on <env> (the apply). Restrict <env> to protected branches.
  2. Copy the values of terraform output github into environment variables: GCP_WIF_PROVIDER, GCP_CI_PUSH_SA, GCP_PLANNER_SA, GCP_DEPLOYER_SA; also GCP_IMAGE_REPOSITORY (terraform output image_repository), TF_STATE_BUCKET and TERRAFORM_TFVARS (the contents of the environment's terraform.tfvars).
  3. Optionally add OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET as a secret of <env>-plan and <env> (an ephemeral variable must be given to both the plan and the apply).

The workload identity provider accepts tokens from your repository only, and each service account trusts exactly one GitHub environment, so a job can never assume more than its environment allows. The very first apply of an environment (which creates these identities) is run by a person.

The perimeter is an organisation-level resource, which project-level grants cannot cover: give the deployer roles/accesscontextmanager.policyEditor and the planner roles/accesscontextmanager.policyReader on the access policy yourself (or use a scoped access policy for the platform's projects). Once the perimeter is enforced, people who run Terraform or read the exec projects' logs from outside it need an access level (vpc_sc.access_levels); the deployer has its own ingress rule.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Bucket names are global. The storage contract names buckets mapi-{env}-{purpose} (mapi_spec.storage.bucket_name), so mapi-prod-data must be free in all of Cloud Storage. If a name is taken, choose a more specific environment name (any name matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,15}$, e.g. acme-prod, as a new envs/ directory).
  • KMS key rings are permanent. Recreating a destroyed environment needs terraform import of its key rings.
  • --traffic-only rollbacks cover the HTTP services only; the orchestrator and the Jobs roll back with a release redeploy.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The alert policies in ops/alerts/cloud-monitoring-alerts.yaml and the Cloud Monitoring dashboard read the mapi_* series from Managed Service for Prometheus. Nothing outside an instance can scrape them: the load balancer routes only /v1, /auth/* and the health checks, and the orchestrator has no ingress at all. So each server workload (api, events, orchestrator) runs a collector sidecar, an OpenTelemetry Collector that scrapes the workload's /metrics over 127.0.0.1 every 30 s with the metrics-token bearer and writes the series to Managed Service for Prometheus. The orchestrator serves its own series (dispatch latency, finalize outcomes, integrity failures, running executions, jobs.run 429s) on 127.0.0.1:9464. The runtime identities already hold roles/monitoring.metricWriter.

Mirror the Google-built collector image into the build project's registry, pin it by digest, and set it per environment:

gcloud artifacts docker images copy \
  us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-ops-agents-artifacts/google-cloud-opentelemetry-collector/otelcol-google:<version> \
  europe-west4-docker.pkg.dev/<build project>/mirror/otelcol-google:<version>
# terraform.tfvars
metrics_collector_image = "europe-west4-docker.pkg.dev/<build project>/mirror/otelcol-google@sha256:<digest>"

Without it, a release still deploys, but Terraform warns (check.metrics_collection) and no mapi_* series reaches Cloud Monitoring. Then the PromQL alerts (integrity failure, STALLED rate, spend caps) can never fire. control.metrics_collector also takes scrape_interval, cpu and memory. The api and events services allocate CPU only while they serve requests, so an idle instance is scraped late; that is acceptable for alerts evaluated over 5 to 15 minutes.

The security-suite series (mapi_security_probe_unexpected) comes from the nightly workflow, which pushes it to the Pushgateway named by the MAPI_PUSHGATEWAY_URL repository secret (ops/README.md).

docs.title: Day-2 operations
docs.text:
Rollback. Two ways:

deploy/gcp/rollback.sh --env prod --list            # recorded releases, newest first
deploy/gcp/rollback.sh --env prod --previous        # redeploy the release before the deployed one
deploy/gcp/rollback.sh --env prod --traffic-only    # seconds: services back to their previous revision

A release rollback goes through deploy.sh (plan, confirmation, apply, smoke test) with --skip-migrate: schema changes only move forward. It is recorded as <UTC timestamp>-<id of the release it redeployed>-rollback.json, and --previous replays the records: retried deploys count once, and after rolling back from a bad release a second --previous goes one release further back instead of returning to the bad one. --traffic-only shifts traffic with gcloud without touching Terraform, for incidents; it leaves the orchestrator and the Jobs as they are, and the next deploy moves traffic to the newest revision again.

Migrations by themselves. deploy/gcp/migrate.sh --env prod --image <server@sha256:...>.

Rotate secrets. Raise control.database.password_version in the environment's main.tf (all three database roles and their connection URLs change in one apply), or control.secret_versions.session_secret (signs everyone out) or token_pepper (invalidates every API token). New Cloud Run revisions pick up the latest secret versions.

Rotate the bundle-signing key. Create a KMS key version, set control.kms_key_version to it and list the previous one in control.kms_trusted_key_versions, then deploy; see ops/runbooks/rotating-keys.md. Dropping a version from the trusted list makes every model it signed fail INTEGRITY_FAILURE.

Add an exec pool. Add an entry to exec_pools, run bootstrap.sh for its project, then deploy.sh. The perimeter, the Logging sink, the image-pull grant and the bootstrap-bucket grant follow automatically.

Tear down dev. KMS keys cannot be deleted (only their versions can be scheduled for destruction), so the two signing keys carry prevent_destroy. Release them from the state first, then destroy; dev has no deletion protection and lets Terraform empty its buckets, while staging and prod refuse:

cd infra/terraform/envs/dev
terraform state list | grep 'google_kms_crypto_key\.' | xargs -n1 terraform state rm
terraform destroy

docs.title: Environment of the Cloud Run workloads
docs.text:
This is the deployment contract between Terraform (modules/control/locals.tf) and mapi-server. Every name is a mapi-server setting (see the configuration reference); tests/infra fails if Terraform sets one the server does not read. Plain values:

Variable Workloads Value MAPI_ENV all Environment name; buckets are mapi-{env}-* MAPI_PROFILE all multi-tenant (the local-process executor refuses it) MAPI_OBJECT_STORE all gcs: real Cloud Storage, URLs signed keylessly MAPI_GCP_PROJECT all Project of the Cloud Storage client MAPI_URL_SIGNER all Service account whose signBlob signs URLs (no key file exists) MAPI_URL_UPLOADER all Service account whose signBlob signs create-only upload policies (run outputs); it may create objects in runs and quarantine but never delete them MAPI_SIGNER, MAPI_KMS_KEY_VERSION all kms and …/cryptoKeyVersions/<control.kms_key_version> of the EC P-256 key that signs bundle manifests MAPI_DB_APP_ROLE, MAPI_DB_SYSTEM_ROLE, MAPI_DB_GATEWAY_ROLE all mapi_app (row-level security), mapi_orchestrator (the platform role, the only RLS bypass) and mapi_gateway (the API's lookups before a tenant is known, RLS applies) MAPI_DEFAULT_RESIDENCY all Residency of the platform tenant and of tenants created without one: the control module's default_residency, else what the dispatch pool's region satisfies (eu for europe-west4) MAPI_TRUSTED_PROXIES all 169.254.0.0/16 (Cloud Run's front end), 35.191.0.0/16 and 130.211.0.0/22 (Google load balancer front ends) and the load balancer's address: the hops skipped when the API reads the caller's address from X-Forwarded-For. Check a sign-up's audit fingerprint differs between two networks after the first deployment; add hops through extra_env if your topology has more MAPI_API_URL, MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN, MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN all, web Public origins (the API shares the app origin behind the load balancer) MAPI_DATA_DIR all /tmp/mapi (in-memory scratch) MAPI_ALLOWED_HOSTS api, events Host names the service answers MAPI_OIDC_ISSUER, MAPI_OIDC_CLIENT_ID api Browser sign-in MAPI_PUBSUB_PUSH_AUDIENCE, MAPI_PUBSUB_PUSH_SERVICE_ACCOUNT, MAPI_PUBSUB_PUSH_SUBSCRIPTIONS events What a valid Pub/Sub push token must say, and the one subscription allowed to push MAPI_EXECUTOR orchestrator cloudrun-jobs MAPI_WORKER_METRICS_PORT, MAPI_WORKER_METRICS_HOST orchestrator 9464 on 127.0.0.1: the orchestrator's own /metrics (dispatch, reconcile, finalize series), for the collector sidecar MAPI_CLOUDRUN_PROJECT, MAPI_CLOUDRUN_REGION orchestrator The exec pool it dispatches to (control.dispatch_pool, default the first non-public pool); its Jobs follow the default mapi-{env}-{base}-{class} names MAPI_BOOTSTRAP_URL Jobs gs://mapi-{env}-bootstrap/{nonce} (set on each Job, read by the runner)

From Secret Manager (references, resolved when a revision starts):

Variable Workloads Secret MAPI_DATABASE_URL api, events db-url-app-direct: mapi_app, direct (the LISTEN that feeds SSE) MAPI_DATABASE_APP_URL api, events, orchestrator db-url-app: mapi_app through the pooler (transaction mode); tenant sessions MAPI_DATABASE_GATEWAY_URL api, events db-url-gateway: mapi_gateway through the pooler; sign-in lookups, operator routes, routing pushed events (no RLS bypass) MAPI_DATABASE_SYSTEM_URL orchestrator db-url-orchestrator: mapi_orchestrator, direct; the orchestrator's loops. Only the orchestrator's service account can read this secret (plan §9) MAPI_DATABASE_URL orchestrator db-url-orchestrator (procrastinate needs LISTEN) MAPI_DATABASE_URL migrate db-url-migrate: role mapi_migrate (schema owner), direct MAPI_SERVER_SECRET all The root of the API-token pepper and the audit fingerprint key; rotating it (control.secret_versions.server_secret) invalidates every API token MAPI_METRICS_TOKEN api, events, orchestrator, collector sidecars The bearer a scraper presents on GET /metrics (the multi-tenant profile refuses scrapes without it) MAPI_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET api Only once a client secret version exists

One orchestrator serves one exec pool, and an environment deploys one orchestrator: runs go only to control.dispatch_pool. Until tier placement across pools (M5), keep every tenant on that pool. A second pool, such as a separate exec project for public tenants, needs a second orchestrator outside this module. Both orchestrators must then set disjoint MAPI_DISPATCH_TIERS, for example internal,self-hosted-trusted,verified through control.extra_env.orchestrator here and public on the other. Without that, leasing is not pool-aware: either orchestrator takes any tenant's queued runs, and public-tier code can land in the paid pool. Terraform's exec_pools[*].public only chooses the default dispatch_pool. The server does not read it.

Each workload can get extra plain variables through control.extra_env in the environment's main.tf; secrets never go there.

docs.title: Testing the infrastructure
docs.text:
uv run pytest tests/infra -q                     # everything below
TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=~/.terraform.d/plugin-cache uv run pytest tests/infra -q   # reuse providers
  • Static invariants (always run): deny-all egress with exactly two exceptions, no public buckets or principals, max_retries = 0 and gen2 on every Job, the VPC-SC perimeter and DNS policy, write-only secrets, digest-pinned images, and agreement with the mapi_spec contracts (bucket names, resource class sizes, runner environment, the push endpoint).
  • terraform fmt, terraform validate for every environment (with -backend=false).
  • terraform test for every module: each is applied against mocked Google providers, so every expression and wiring is evaluated, and the security properties are asserted on the resulting values (no credentials, no cloud calls).
  • Deploy scripts: --help, argument checks, the confirmation guard and full dry runs, with stub terraform/gcloud/docker/curl binaries that prove nothing executes; under /bin/bash 3.2 and the bash on PATH. shellcheck runs when installed.

The Terraform tests are skipped when terraform is not installed; the first run downloads the Google providers (about 250 MB, into a temporary cache unless TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR is set).

docs.title: Container images v0.2
docs.text:
The platform ships as six images (plus a worker target), built from images/<name>/Dockerfile with the repository root as the build context. They exist to run the exact production artifacts locally (Docker Compose), to back the docker executor, and to become the Cloud Run Jobs in v0.3.

make docker-build                      # every image, tagged mapi/<name>:<version>
make docker-build IMAGES="server web"  # a subset
make docker-pin-check                  # every base image pinned by digest?

docs.title: The images
docs.text:
Image Contents Runs as Entry point mapi/base-bayes mapi-runner, SDK, steps, plot recipes, mapi-pymc, the mmm.* and tabular.* plugins, a C++ compiler for PyTensor 10001 mapi-runner mapi/base-ml mapi-runner, SDK, steps, plot recipes, mapi-sklearn (sklearn.* plugins). No PyMC. 10001 mapi-runner mapi/base-forecast mapi-runner, SDK, steps, plot recipes, mapi-pymc, the ts.* plugins 10001 mapi-runner mapi/worker base-bayes plus the ts.* plugins and mapi-server (target worker of the base-bayes Dockerfile); for compose only 10001 mapi-server worker mapi/server The control plane: mapi-server, mapi-spec, the JSON-only mapi-plots core, docker-py. No science dependencies. 10001 mapi-server api (or worker, migrate) mapi/gcs-shim The local Cloud Storage emulator 10001 mapi-gcs-shim mapi/web nginx serving apps/web (port 8080) and apps/plot-sandbox (port 8081) 101 nginx

make docker-build IMAGES="server web" builds a subset. make docker-build builds them all, plus mapi/worker whenever base-bayes is in the set. Every image is labelled with the OCI title, version, revision (git commit) and created keys.

docs.title: How the Python images are built
docs.text:
Every Python image uses the same multi-stage pattern:

  1. manifests copies the build context and deletes everything except pyproject.toml and uv.lock files. Its output changes only when dependencies change.
  2. builder installs the third-party dependencies of the image's package set from those manifests alone (uv sync --frozen --no-install-workspace, once per package, into /opt/mapi/venv). BuildKit caches this layer, so editing source code does not reinstall PyMC. The builder then copies the sources and installs the workspace packages themselves, non-editable. Every version comes from uv.lock.
  3. runtime starts again from the same python:3.12-slim base, adds tini (and g++ for the PyMC images), creates user 10001, and copies in only the virtual environment. The images that run mapi-server (mapi/server and mapi/worker) also copy uv.lock to /opt/mapi/uv.lock and set MAPI_UV_LOCK_PATH to it. Its SHA-256 is the image digest that the API and the orchestrator cache the step and model catalog under, the same value make dev computes. Both images are built from one lock, so api and worker agree.

The package set is the MAPI_PACKAGES build argument. images/common/install_packages.py turns it into uv sync calls. The xgboost dependency nvidia-nccl-cu13, a 300 MB wheel used only for multi-GPU training, is never installed (MAPI_NO_INSTALL).

docs.title: Build-time guards
docs.text:
An image that is not what it claims to be fails to build:

  • Package assertions. images/common/assert_dists.py checks MAPI_ASSERT_PRESENT and MAPI_ASSERT_ABSENT against the real environment. For example, base-ml must not contain pymc, pytensor or numba, and server must not contain numpy, xarray, pandas, scipy, pyarrow, PyMC, mapi_sdk, mapi_runner or any plugin.
  • Import contracts in the control-plane image. The contracts stage of images/server/Dockerfile installs import-linter (hash-pinned from uv.lock) into a throwaway copy of the environment, and runs the repository's contracts against the packages exactly as installed. The runtime stage depends on that stage, so BuildKit cannot skip it.
  • Catalog export. The runner images load every installed step, model and plot plugin and write /opt/mapi/catalog.json with its digest (/opt/mapi/catalog.digest). If no steps or models are registered, the build fails.

The same claims are also proven without Docker: tests/devops/test_container_invariants.py computes each image's dependency closure from uv.lock (scripts/lock_closure.py) and checks it against the assertions.

docs.title: Compile caches and the read-only root filesystem
docs.text:
PyTensor compiles C at run time, and Numba caches machine code. Both caches are warmed during the build by compiling a small hierarchical model, then baked read-only into /opt/mapi/cache. PyTensor needs a writable compile directory, because it takes a lock and adds new modules. So at start-up the entry point (images/common/runner-entrypoint.sh) builds a symlink farm of the baked cache under /tmp/mapi-cache: real directories, with files that are symlinks to the baked objects. This costs a few KiB of RAM, which matters on Cloud Run's in-memory filesystem, and PyTensor accepts the relocated entries without recompiling.

HOME, PYTENSOR_FLAGS, NUMBA_CACHE_DIR and MPLCONFIGDIR all point under /tmp. The first three are on the runner's worker-environment allow-list (mapi_spec.run.WORKER_ENV_ALLOWLIST), so plugin code sees them after the supervisor scrubs the environment. The result is that every image runs with --read-only and a tmpfs on /tmp.

docker run mapi/base-bayes runs the runner. Arguments starting with - are passed to the runner, and any other command replaces it (docker run mapi/base-bayes python -c ...).

docs.title: The web image and the plot sandbox
docs.text:
mapi/web builds both Vite apps with pnpm, using --frozen-lockfile and --ignore-scripts, so no package lifecycle scripts run. It serves them from one unprivileged nginx with two server blocks. NGINX_ENVSUBST_TEMPLATE_DIR selects which blocks are rendered: /etc/nginx/templates/all (the default), web or plots. Origins are runtime settings rendered into the headers at start-up.

App (:8080, MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN) Plot sandbox (:8081, MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN) CSP default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' (no unsafe-eval, no inline scripts); frame-src = the plots origin; connect-src = self, MAPI_API_URL, MAPI_GCS_ENDPOINT; frame-ancestors 'none' default-src 'none'; scripts, styles and images from its own origin only; connect-src = its own /topojson/ only; frame-ancestors = the app origin Other headers X-Frame-Options: DENY, nosniff, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, COOP and CORP same-origin, Trusted Types in report-only mode nosniff, no-referrer, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * API access /v1/ is proxied to MAPI_API_UPSTREAM, unbuffered with a one-hour read timeout for SSE None: no proxy, and the CSP blocks it

The sandbox documents are framed with sandbox="allow-scripts" and no same-origin access, so they have an opaque origin. Their module scripts, styles and topojson are therefore fetched in CORS mode. That is why the sandbox answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *; the assets are static and public, and no cookies are involved. It is also why its CSP lists the plots origin explicitly next to 'self'.

MAPI_WEB_SCRIPT_SRC_EXTRA (empty by default) adds sources to the app's script-src. Use it only after a review, for example if a library needs 'wasm-unsafe-eval'. Trusted Types are in report-only mode until the SPA ships its policy.

docs.title: Base images and pinning
docs.text:
Every base image is a build argument with a readable tag and a digest:

ARG PYTHON_IMAGE=python:3.12-slim-trixie@sha256:a6e3…11b1

The Dockerfile frontend (# syntax=) and the compose postgres image are pinned the same way. make docker-pin re-resolves every tag through the registry API. It needs no Docker daemon, and you should review the resulting diff like any dependency bump. make docker-pin-check (also run in CI and by make release-check) fails if anything is unpinned.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml builds every image, plus the worker target, on each push and pull request, using the GitHub Actions layer cache. Images are never pushed. A separate job checks the digest pins and validates both compose files with docker compose config.

With the images built and a Docker daemon running, uv run pytest tests/devops/test_compose_smoke.py -m docker boots postgres, gcs-shim, migrate, api and worker under a throw-away project name. It publishes no host ports. It then checks that api and worker started and that they agree on the values bundle verification depends on: the image digest and the bundle-signing key.

docs.title: Local, without Docker v0.2
docs.text:
make dev runs the whole platform on your machine without Docker. PostgreSQL comes from the pgserver wheel and object storage from the GCS shim, so the only requirements are the uv workspace and, for the web app, Node.js with pnpm.

make install          # uv sync --all-packages (+ pnpm install once apps/ exist)
make dev              # start everything; Ctrl-C stops everything
make seed             # in another shell: load the E33 demo data and spec
open http://127.0.0.1:5173

The quickstart walks through fitting, inspecting and scoring the demo model from the browser. This page explains what make dev runs, how to work on one component, and where local state lives.

docs.title: Signing in v0.3
docs.text:
make dev runs the servers in the dev profile: multi-tenant, with a development identity provider built into the API. The browser shows a sign-in screen. Choose one of the seeded accounts on the provider's page:

Account Role admin@dev.local Admin of the default tenant and a platform operator (the admin console) analyst@dev.local runner in the default project viewer@dev.local viewer in the default project

make seed and make e2e sign in by themselves as admin@dev.local (change it with MAPI_DEV_ACCOUNT). The CLI signs in with mapi login --issuer https://dev-idp.mapi.localhost --discovery-url http://127.0.0.1:8000/dev/idp. Anyone who can reach the API can sign in as any of these accounts, which is why the profile exists only for local development. MAPI_STACK_PROFILE=single-tenant make dev gives back the credential-less v0.2 API. See Authentication and isolation for the details.

docs.title: Signing up v0.4
docs.text: Self-service sign-up (POST /auth/signup) is on in the dev profile. Its e-mails are not sent: the dev mailer writes each one to an outbox under MAPI_DATA_DIR/outbox, and make outbox prints the newest ones with their verification links (TO=<address> keeps one recipient's). The API serves the same at GET /dev/outbox?to=<address>. A verified sign-up creates a public-tier workspace; to sign in to it, sign up with one of the seeded addresses above, because the development identity provider only knows those. A public workspace runs built-in models and declarative specs only, and only on an executor with enforced egress and DNS, so the local-process executor of make dev refuses its runs (cut line A; see Sign-up and abuse controls).

docs.title: What make dev starts
docs.text:
scripts/dev.py is a small process supervisor. It starts each service in dependency order and waits until the service is ready before starting the ones that need it. All output goes to one terminal, with each line prefixed by its service name (coloured when the output is a terminal).

flowchart LR
    pg[(postgres<br/>.local/pg)] --> migrate
    shim[gcs-shim<br/>:4443] --> api
    migrate --> api[api<br/>:8000]
    migrate --> worker
    shim --> worker
    api --> web[web<br/>:5173]
    plots[plots<br/>:5174]
Service Command Ready when postgres Embedded PostgreSQL 16 (pgserver), data in .local/pg, unix socket only. Skipped when DATABASE_URL is set. pg_ctl reports it running and the mapi database exists gcs-shim mapi-gcs-shim serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4443 --cors-origin <web origin> --root .local/gcs The port accepts connections migrate mapi-server migrate (runs once) It exits with status 0 api mapi-server api --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 GET /healthz returns 2xx worker mapi-server worker with MAPI_EXECUTOR=local-process: dispatcher, reconciler, event ingestion and the finalizer queue. Every run is a mapi-runner supervisor process that starts its own worker process. Started web pnpm --filter @mapi/web dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5173 --strictPort The port accepts connections plots pnpm --filter @mapi/plot-sandbox dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5174 --strictPort The port accepts connections

Every service receives the same resolved environment: MAPI_ENV, DATABASE_URL, MAPI_GCS_ENDPOINT, MAPI_API_URL, MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN, MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN and MAPI_DATA_DIR. The values come from mapi_spec.localdev.LocalDev, the same contract the services themselves read, so they cannot disagree about ports. The configuration reference lists every variable.

The plot sandbox is a separate origin

Plots render in an <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts"> served from MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN (port 5174), never from the app origin (port 5173). LocalDev refuses a configuration that puts both on the same origin.

docs.title: Shutting down
docs.text:
Ctrl+C (or make stop from another shell) stops the services in reverse start order. Each service runs in its own process group. The supervisor sends that group SIGTERM, and sends SIGKILL if it is still running after the grace period (10 s, --grace to change). Child processes such as Vite's esbuild are stopped with their parent. A second Ctrl+C kills everything at once. The embedded PostgreSQL is stopped last, unless you ran scripts/dev.py up --keep-db.

If any long-running service exits on its own, the supervisor stops the whole stack and exits with a non-zero status. It never restarts anything silently: the log above the shutdown shows the reason.

docs.title: The first start
docs.text:
On its first start against a new environment the worker logs no catalog for sha256:…: queued describe run. The catalog (the steps, models and plot recipes installed in the runner, with their settings schemas and schema effects) is produced by a sandboxed describe run of the real runner and cached per uv.lock digest, so it is rebuilt only when the locked dependencies change. Until it is ready, spec validation reports the catalog as unavailable; it takes a few seconds.

Runs use the same isolation as in production, minus what a laptop cannot do: the run event DEV_MODE_ISOLATION notes that the worker process runs as your user, without a uid split or no_new_privs.

Plugin code runs as you, next to the platform's keys

Without a uid split, run code (plugins and the steps they load) can read every file your user can. That includes the shim's control key (.local/gcs/_shim/keys/control.json, full access to every bucket), the bundle-signing key (.local/keys/) and the executions directory. So a hostile plugin could forge a signed bundle or rewrite outputs after the finalizer checked them. The orchestrator makes itself non-dumpable on Linux, so run code cannot read its environment (DATABASE_URL) or its memory. The worker logs the same warning when it starts. Only run plugin code you trust in make dev.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
Command What it does make dev (or make run) Start the stack in the foreground make dev ONLY=api Start api and what it depends on (gcs-shim, migrate) make dev WITHOUT=web,plots Everything except the two Vite servers (for example while the web app is not built yet) make stop Stop a stack running in another shell, then its embedded PostgreSQL make status Which services are up, and whether PostgreSQL is running make migrate Apply database migrations once. It starts the embedded PostgreSQL if needed and stops it again afterwards. make db-shell psql on the dev database (the embedded server or DATABASE_URL) make seed Load the E33 demo datasets and the eu-geo-mmm spec through the HTTP API (make seed SIZE=full for the large variant) make e2e The end-to-end suites against the running stack: pytest -m e2e (tests/e2e, through the Python client), then the Playwright @e2e suite (apps/web/e2e, through the browser) make outbox The dev mailer's newest e-mails and their links (sign-up verification); TO=<address> filters make clean-local Delete MAPI_DATA_DIR (database, objects, supervisor state). It refuses while anything is running; YES=1 skips the prompt. uv run python scripts/dev.py env Print the resolved environment as export lines, for running a component by hand

make seed uses only the public API. It creates the datasets eu_media_daily, fx_daily and holidays_eu, uploads each table to the signed URL the API returns, waits for the sandboxed ingest runs, then creates the spec pointing at the new dataset versions. Running it again adds new dataset versions and a new spec revision. The datasets themselves are reused. SIZE is only read from the make command line: some toolchains (conda's compilers) export a SIZE variable of their own.

uv run python scripts/seed.py --export demo/ writes the same tables, the E33 score payloads and the spec as files instead, for uploading through the web app.

docs.title: End-to-end tests
docs.text:
make e2e drives the M1 flow through the running stack: upload the E33 data, validate and fit the spec, follow the run over SSE, check the signed manifest and the bundle, score an 8-week forecast, a new market, a weekly EUR plan and counterfactuals, and probe the security boundaries that are visible from outside (the bootstrap object is gone, forged events are refused, the plot iframe is an opaque origin). Start make dev first; both suites read the same MAPI_* variables, so export them in the shell that runs make e2e when you moved a port. The browser suite writes screenshots to apps/web/e2e/screenshots/ (git-ignored).

export MAPI_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8010   # only if you moved the API
make dev                                     # shell 1
make e2e                                     # shell 2: about 25 minutes

make e2e also runs the M2 tenancy suite and the M3 suites: the trust lifecycle and the whole Guided journey to an endpoint, webhooks, embeds, Atlas, export and deletion (see M3 verification). Two settings make the deletion checks complete: start the stack with MAPI_TENANT_DELETION_GRACE_S=0 (no grace period) and, on a fresh MAPI_DATA_DIR, MAPI_BUNDLE_RETENTION_DAYS=0 (no retention lock on model bundles). Otherwise those checks stop where the platform waits and are skipped. Each run signs up two workspaces; the default sign-up limits (5 per address and hour, 25 per dev.local and day) allow two runs an hour, so raise MAPI_SIGNUP_PER_IP_PER_HOUR and MAPI_SIGNUP_PER_DOMAIN_PER_DAY on a stack you test repeatedly. The Atlas step uses Atlas itself when ATLAS_DIR (default ../optimizer-framework) holds a checkout.

Webhooks reach receivers on your machine: in the dev profile make dev writes a throwaway CA and a certificate for 127.0.0.1 and localhost to $MAPI_DATA_DIR/dev/webhook-tls/ and the servers trust it and allow both hosts. Serve HTTPS with cert.pem and key.pem from there and register https://127.0.0.1:<port>/....

The mocked Playwright smoke suite (pnpm --filter @mapi/web test) serves its own build on port 5173, so run it while make dev is stopped.

docs.title: Working on one component
docs.text:
To run a component yourself, for example with a debugger or auto-reload, either exclude it and start it by hand with the same environment:

make dev WITHOUT=api,web           # web depends on api, so exclude it too
eval "$(uv run python scripts/dev.py env)"
mapi-server api --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

or replace its command with MAPI_DEV_<NAME>_CMD. The command is shell-quoted; <NAME> is GCS_SHIM, MIGRATE, API, WORKER, WEB or PLOTS:

MAPI_DEV_API_CMD="uvicorn mapi_server.app:app --reload --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000" make dev

The readiness probe still applies, so a replacement api must answer GET /healthz.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
make dev reads your shell environment. It does not read .env, which is only for docker compose. With nothing set, everything uses the defaults above. To change something, export the variable first:

export MAPI_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9000          # move the API (and its probe) to port 9000
export DATABASE_URL=postgresql://me@localhost/mapi  # use your own PostgreSQL instead of pgserver
make dev

Export the same MAPI_* URLs in every shell that talks to the stack (make seed, make e2e, the CLI, the Python client). The configuration reference lists every variable, including those that only compose or the images use.

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text:
All local state lives under MAPI_DATA_DIR, which defaults to .local/ in the repository root and is ignored by git.

.local/
├─ pg/                    PostgreSQL data directory (pgserver); log in pg/log
├─ gcs/                   GCS shim objects (buckets mapi-local-*)
│  └─ _shim/keys/         the shim's principals: control.json (control plane), exec.json (runs)
├─ keys/                  bundle-signing-p256.pem: signs bundle manifests (stands in for KMS)
├─ outbox/                the dev mailer's e-mails (make outbox, GET /dev/outbox)
├─ executions/            per-run scratch of the local executor (removed when a run ends)
└─ dev/supervisor.json    pid of the running supervisor and its services (make stop/status)

Deleting keys/ makes every registered model version unusable: their manifests no longer verify, so the API refuses to mint download links for them (INTEGRITY_FAILURE).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Port conflicts, a stale supervisor, PostgreSQL that will not start, failed migrations, an API that never becomes ready and blank plots are covered in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: M2 verification v0.3
docs.text:
Milestone M2 (cloud and multi-tenant core) has five exit criteria:

  1. 100 concurrent fits without loss;
  2. chaos and executor conformance green;
  3. the security suite green nightly;
  4. p95 time-to-RUNNING under 90 s;
  5. per-run cost shown in the UI.

This page records how far each one was verified locally and what still needs a real Google Cloud project. The local run had no Docker daemon and no cloud credentials:

  • Cloud Storage was the GCS shim;
  • Postgres was the embedded pgserver;
  • the Cloud Run Jobs executor ran against its in-memory fake Admin API (FakeCloudRun);
  • Pub/Sub pushes were simulated with locally signed OIDC tokens;
  • Terraform was validated, never applied.

Verified on 2026-10-15 at commit feat/m2-e2e (v0.3 development), on an Apple-silicon laptop (8 cores, 16 GB, macOS).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Exit criterion Verified locally Result Still needs real GCP 100 concurrent fits without loss make load-test: 100 fits through the real dispatcher, reconciler, finalizer and events path on the Cloud Run executor (fake Admin API) and the GCS shim. A second mode keeps all 100 executions live at once. A burst of 32 real fits ran on the live dev stack. 100/100 succeeded, one execution and one attempt per run. 32/32 real fits succeeded, with one attempt, ledger entry and model version per run. The same burst on Cloud Run Jobs (real cold starts, real jobs.run quota) Chaos green make chaos 5/5 passed Cloud SQL failover; Pub/Sub redelivery from the real subscription Executor conformance green 12 cases on fake-cloudrun and on local-process, plus the gate 24 passed, 3 skipped (documented capabilities local-process lacks), 0 failed The 12 cases against the real Cloud Run Admin API (no live target exists yet, see below) Security suite nightly green make security-suite EXECUTOR=local-process. The nightly workflow is written. PASS: all 17 outcomes acceptable for PROCESS Probes inside a gVisor container (needs Docker) and inside a Cloud Run Jobs execution (MICROVM) p95 time-to-RUNNING < 90 s Measured in the load test, and on the live stack Fake Cloud Run: p95 45.9–46.5 s (100 fits). Live local stack: p95 3.0 s (16 real fits) and 8.9 s (32) Real cold start of a ~2.5 GB base image [verify M0] comes on top (see the warning below) Per-run cost shown in the UI Playwright against the live stack: the run page, the runs list and the usage page show the metered cost $0.0003 metered on the run page and in the list; usage totals match the ledger The price table against real Cloud Run billing

Multi-tenancy, which the M2 scope adds, was also verified end to end on the live stack:

  • two users in two tenants, signed in through the development identity provider;
  • cross-tenant access refused at the API and by row-level security;
  • token scopes;
  • quotas;
  • the spend-cap kill switch, held at dispatch;
  • per-run cost;
  • the audit trail.

p95 time-to-RUNNING on real Cloud Run

For a burst of 100 fits, the 46 s p95 comes almost entirely from the submit rate: MAPI_CLOUDRUN_SUBMITS_PER_MINUTE=150 (the regional jobs.run quota is 180 a minute, [verify M0]) spreads 100 submissions over about 40 s. The fake provisions in 0.3–1.5 s. On Cloud Run, every execution's cold start adds to that. If the p95 cold start of a base image is over about 40 s, a cold 100-fit burst misses the 90 s budget even though every single fit starts quickly. Measure the cold start first (see What remains for real GCP). Homogeneous fan-out (sweeps, SBC) avoids the limit by using one execution with taskCount; independent fits cannot.

docs.title: Load: 100 concurrent fits
docs.text:
make load-test                                    # default: fits of 0.2–3 s
LOAD_TEST_FIT_MS=40000-60000 make load-test       # 40–60 s fits: all 100 live at once

packages/server/tests/test_load_cloudrun.py submits 100 fits. They go through the production rate limits: the dispatcher's token bucket and the executor's 150 a minute. The backend misbehaves on purpose:

  • it answers the first jobs.run calls with 429;
  • it loses two responses, which leaves orphans the executor must adopt instead of resubmitting.

A synthetic supervisor reads its bootstrap object and writes its outputs through signed URLs on the real GCS shim. Its events arrive as OIDC-authenticated Pub/Sub pushes, with random lag and 5 % duplicates.

Mode Runs p50 / p95 / max time-to-RUNNING Most executions live at once Pushes (duplicates) Wall default 100/100 succeeded 28.95 / 46.45 / 48.53 s 9 525 (24) 50.5 s LOAD_TEST_FIT_MS=40000-60000 100/100 succeeded 28.47 / 45.93 / 48.09 s 100 525 (24) 105.8 s

Both modes asserted exactly one execution and one attempt per run (no double dispatch), and that every run succeeded (no loss).

Real fits on the live stack. This is opt-in, because each fit is a pair of processes on the host:

make dev   # with the MAPI_* ports below
MAPI_E2E_BURST_RUNS=32 uv run pytest -q -s -m e2e tests/e2e/test_m2_burst_stack.py
Burst Result p50 / p95 / max time-to-RUNNING p95 queued → finished 16 real store-demand fits 16/16 succeeded 1.32 / 3.0 / 3.23 s 38.3 s 32 real store-demand fits 32/32 succeeded 3.66 / 8.91 / 9.61 s 82.0 s

For each run, the test checked that it has exactly one row in each of run_attempts, cost_ledger and model_versions (counted straight in Postgres), and that it registered a distinct model version.

docs.title: Chaos
docs.text:
make chaos

5/5 passed:

  • the worker killed during PROVISIONING;
  • the worker killed during RUNNING;
  • event redelivery and reordering;
  • a redelivered event with a bad HMAC that never advances the run;
  • a Postgres restart mid-run.

Each converged to the correct terminal state with no lost or duplicated attempt.

docs.title: Executor conformance
docs.text:
uv run pytest -q -rs packages/server/tests/test_executor_conformance.py

24 passed, 3 skipped. The 12 cases are:

  • submit;
  • orphan adoption after a dispatcher crash;
  • duplicate-submit safety;
  • cancel mid-run;
  • timeout;
  • STALLED without a false LOST;
  • confirmed cancel before retry;
  • checkpoint resume;
  • OOM classification;
  • fan-out with taskCount;
  • generation verification;
  • 429 back-off.

Every case passed on fake-cloudrun. The gate test (test_conformance_report_gates_the_executor) passed for both backends.

On local-process, three cases were skipped. They need capabilities that executor does not declare: memory_limit, fanout and remote_control_api. The gate requires exactly those skips.

The 12 cases of the docker backend were deselected, because there is no Docker daemon.

docs.title: Security suite
docs.text:
make security-suite EXECUTOR=local-process

Result: PASS: all 17 probe outcomes acceptable for this executor, and the suite's own tests passed (9). The outcomes match the expected matrix for PROCESS isolation, where either outcome is accepted for the isolation probes but every platform probe must be blocked:

Probe Category Outcome metadata_token, http_egress, dns_egress isolation blocked (no metadata server or egress on this host) write_outside_scratch, reuse_foreign_url, pth_injection, fork_bomb, memory_bomb, disk_bomb, log_flood isolation allowed (accepted: PROCESS is not a security boundary) read_proc1_environ, read_supervisor_mem isolation skipped (no procfs on macOS) forged_stdout_event, tampered_manifest, redos_schema, plot_xss_exfil, reuse_foreign_manifest platform blocked

The probes clean up after themselves: the .pth file and the file written outside scratch were removed.

Two defects in the suite were fixed along the way:

  • The docker and gVisor runner ran python -m mapi_security in the runner image, which never contains the suite. The suite is now mounted read-only into the probe container.
  • --executor cloud used to probe whatever host ran it. It now refuses to run outside a Cloud Run Jobs execution.

.github/workflows/nightly.yml schedules the following jobs every night:

  • chaos;
  • executor conformance;
  • both load-test modes;
  • the security suite on local-process;
  • the security suite inside gVisor (it installs runsc and builds the worker image).

The workflow was checked as YAML here; it has not run on GitHub yet.

docs.title: Multi-tenancy through the live stack
docs.text:
make e2e    # API suites (M1 + M2), then the browser @e2e suites

The M2 API suite, tests/e2e/test_m2_tenancy_stack.py (11 tests, about 2 minutes), runs the following steps:

  1. The platform operator creates two internal tenants. Each has an invited admin, the dev accounts analyst@dev.local and viewer@dev.local.
  2. Each admin signs in, which claims the invitation, and creates project growth.
  3. Each admin uploads data under the same dataset names, fits the corpus's scikit-learn store-demand model and scores it.

On that state, the suite proves the following.

Sign-in

  • The BFF flow works: /auth/login, the IdP, then /auth/callback, with PKCE S256.
  • A replayed callback gets 401.
  • A cookie mutation without X-CSRF-Token, or from a foreign origin, gets 403.
  • Logout ends the session.
  • ID-token bearers work.
  • API tokens work, are bound to their project, and are dead (401) after revocation.

API isolation. The other tenant always gets 404 or 403, never a 2xx or a 5xx:

  • on 18 project-scoped reads: datasets and versions, the preview, the data artifact, specs, runs, logs, run plots, models, versions, artifacts, ui/ views and plots;
  • on the SSE stream;
  • on 10 writes: cancel, retry, resume, spec revision, dry-run, score, evaluate, fit, upload and new version;
  • on tenant routes: tenant, projects, members, audit and usage;
  • when the caller names the other tenant's project explicitly.

Lists never show the other tenant's rows. The same dataset://growth/... ref resolves to each tenant's own data: the lineage dataset hashes differ.

Row-level security, straight in Postgres (as mapi_app)

  • FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is on for every table checked.
  • A fresh connection without a tenant fails closed.
  • With app.tenant_id set, each table shows the caller's own rows and none of the other tenant's.
  • The other tenant's run is neither visible nor updatable by id.
  • Moving a row to another tenant violates the policy.
  • The setting is transaction-local: after commit, a pooled connection sees nothing.

Scopes

  • A models:read token can read but gets 403 on fit, score and token minting, and on another tenant's project.
  • A runs:create token fits, and the audit log attributes the run to that token.

Quotas. Both answer 429 QUOTA_EXCEEDED, and the other tenant is unaffected:

  • a tenant cap of vcpu_seconds_per_day=1;
  • a token's vcpu_seconds_budget=1.

Kill switch. This test briefly pauses the worker (SIGSTOP) so a run is deterministically queued first. Then:

  • the operator makes the tenant verified and sets global_spend_cap_micros=1;
  • the queued run stays queued across several dispatcher polls, so it is held at dispatch;
  • new runs of that tenant get 429 with the spend-cap message;
  • an internal tenant keeps being admitted and dispatched;
  • once the tenant is internal again, the held run is leased and succeeds.

Cost. For every fit and score:

  • Run.cost is metered (estimated=false, one attempt billed, amount_micros > 0, a price version, and vCPU- and GiB-seconds);
  • there is one actual ledger row per attempt, in the right tenant;
  • GET /v1/usage and the tenant usage add up to at least the ledger.

Audit

  • The tenant log has project.create, run.create, token.create and token.revoke.
  • The platform log has tenant.create, quota.update, kill_switch.update and auth.login.
  • The other tenant cannot read the log.

docs.title: The browser flow
docs.text:
MAPI_E2E=1 pnpm --filter @mapi/web exec playwright test e2e/m2-flow.e2e.spec.ts

Chromium runs the M2 browser flow, apps/web/e2e/m2-flow.e2e.spec.ts (4 tests):

  1. Sign-in through the IdP's account chooser.
  2. The tenant switcher: switch to the seeded tenant; the choice survives a reload.
  3. Fit from the spec editor and wait for succeeded. The run page shows Metered · price table … · 1 attempt billed and cost $0.0003; the runs list and the usage page show the cost too.
  4. Mint a models:read token, then revoke it. Before revocation, the API refuses it a fit (403); after revocation, the token gets 401.
  5. Admin console:
    1. make the tenant verified;
    2. set a spend cap;
    3. the tenant admin's next fit is refused with the spend-cap message;
    4. remove the cap (typing REMOVE);
    5. find kill_switch.update and tenant.update in the audit log.

tests/e2e/m2_browser_seed.py seeds the tenant and puts the stack back afterwards. The screenshots in apps/web/e2e/screenshots/m2-*.png (git-ignored) were reviewed. They led to these fixes:

  • Sub-cent costs showed as $0.00. A 3 s ingest cost $0.000047, and the spend-cap badge for a 1-micro cap read "$0.00 per day". Amounts below $0.0001 now keep two significant digits.
  • Session usage was listed as "-" in "By token". The server's group key is -; the page now labels it "Signed-in users".
  • Memory showed "0 GiB·h". It is now in GiB-seconds under an hour.
  • A finished run without output said "No output captured yet".
  • The project switcher truncated tenant and project names even on wide screens.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
make tf-validate

87 passed, 1 skipped: shellcheck is not installed. This covers:

  • terraform fmt;
  • validate of every environment, with -backend=false;
  • module tests with mocked providers;
  • the HCL invariants (for example digest-pinned images, the deny-all egress, the env-only overrides);
  • the deploy scripts and the deploy workflow.

docs.title: Local stack used
docs.text:
The API's default port was taken, so the stack ran on other ports, with a fresh data directory and two extra dev accounts:

export MAPI_API_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18000 MAPI_GCS_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:14443 \
       MAPI_WEB_ORIGIN=http://127.0.0.1:15173 MAPI_PLOTS_ORIGIN=http://127.0.0.1:15174 \
       MAPI_DATA_DIR=$PWD/.local/m2e2e VITE_API_BASE=http://127.0.0.1:18000
make dev                     # dev profile: dev IdP, the default tenant, admin@dev.local as operator
make e2e                     # in another shell, with the same exports

MAPI_E2E_ACCOUNTS selects the two tenant admins of the API suite (default analyst@dev.local,viewer@dev.local). MAPI_E2E_UI_ACCOUNT selects the browser flow's tenant admin (default analyst@dev.local). Both suites need a stack in the dev profile, and skip otherwise.
